# Part 1: Master Project Overview & Chronological Timeline

# Municipal Meeting Records & Chronological Timeline: 100 Beal Street Senior Affordable Housing

<!-- v2 – Comprehensive verified timeline and municipal meeting records index -->

This record compiles all verified municipal public hearings, executive sessions, votes, board deliberations, and Town Meeting warrants concerning **100 Beal Street Senior Affordable Housing** (School Tract II) across the **Hingham Housing Authority (HHA)**, **Hingham Select Board / Board of Selectmen**, **Conservation Commission**, **Planning Board**, **Affordable Housing Trust**, and **Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA)** from 1989 through 2026.

---

| **March 7, 1989** | Hingham Board of Selectmen / HHA | Municipal Conveyance | School Tract II Land Conveyance | Selectmen conveyed 15.014 acres (School Tract II) to HHA (Book 9097, Page 158) with restriction for adolescent residential educational facility. | [`Hingham_Beal_Street_Deed_1989_and_ZBA_Decision.pdf`](../documents/Hingham_Beal_Street_Deed_1989_and_ZBA_Decision.pdf) |
| **June 12, 2001** | Hingham Board of Selectmen & HHA | Memorandum of Agreement | School Tract II Demolition & Infrastructure | Executed MOU under which Town funded demolition and site prep in anticipation of returning excess acreage to Town. | Cited in 2019 Minutes |
| **May 8, 2006** | Hingham Annual Town Meeting | Legislative Town Meeting | **Article 38:** Amendment of 1989 Deed Restriction on School Tract II | Town voted to amend 1989 deed restriction on School Tract II (15.014 acres) to authorize **"residential development which includes affordable housing that qualifies for inclusion on the Subsidized Housing Inventory (SHI)."** | [`Hingham_Town_Meeting_Warrant_2006_Article_38_School_Tract_II.pdf`](../documents/Hingham_Town_Meeting_Warrant_2006_Article_38_School_Tract_II.pdf)<br>[`Hingham_Town_Meeting_2006_Beal_St_Amended_Deed_Vote.pdf`](../documents/Hingham_Town_Meeting_2006_Beal_St_Amended_Deed_Vote.pdf) |

| **Sept 20, 2017**<br>7:00 PM | Hingham Select Board | Regular Public Meeting | Selectmen's Parcel & 100 Beal Street Senior Housing Update | Executive Director Sharon Napier presented proposal for 55+ senior affordable apartments; reviewed pending expiration of deed restriction; discussed veteran and local preference. | [`Select_Board_Minutes_2017-09-20_100_Beal.pdf`](Select_Board_Minutes_2017-09-20_100_Beal.pdf) |
| **Feb 8, 2018**<br>1:00 PM | Hingham Housing Authority | Board of Commissioners Meeting | Evaluation of 100 Beal Street Rights and Potential Transfer | Commissioner Lauter moved to engage municipal legal counsel to evaluate 100 Beal Street rights before acting on Town land transfer request. **Passed 3–0**. | [`Select_Board_Minutes_2018-02-08_100_Beal.pdf`](Select_Board_Minutes_2018-02-08_100_Beal.pdf) |

Selectmen voted unanimously (**3–0**) to file litigation against HHA to compel specific performance. | [`Select_Board_Executive_Session_Minutes_2019-02-26_100_Beal.pdf`](Select_Board_Executive_Session_Minutes_2019-02-26_100_Beal.pdf) |
| **June 5, 2019** | Hingham Housing Authority | Special Board Meeting | Transfer of School Tract II Acreage to Town | Under litigation pressure, HHA voted to transfer excess land back to Town. Prompted immediate intervention by DHCD asserting M.G.L. c. 121B, § 34 state jurisdiction. | Reference in Legal Report |
| **July 9, 2019**<br>7:00 PM | Hingham Housing Authority | Regular Board Meeting | 100 Beal Street Transfer & Resident Inquiries | Chair O'Meara and Commissioner Suchecki addressed resident questions regarding 18-year agreement and Town demolition costs; delivered transmittal letter and Quitclaim Deed copy to Town Selectmen. | [`HHA_Minutes_2019-07-09_100_Beal_School_Tract_II.pdf`](HHA_Minutes_2019-07-09_100_Beal_School_Tract_II.pdf) |

5-0.

Recommended Findings of Fact
A. The Commission has found the invasive species management project qualifies as an Ecological
Restoration Limited Project under 310 CMR 10.53(4)(e)(5) as the proposed activities will improve the
natural capacity of a Resource Area(s) to protect the interests identified in M.G.L. c. 131, § 40. The
proposal is for the removal of aquatic nuisance vegetation, Phragmites, to retard pond and lake
eutrophication and will also result in an improvement to habitat value and re-naturalization of the
riparian corridor.
B. The work described in the Ecological Restoration Notice of Intent is within Areas Subject to Protection
under the Wetlands Protection Act, M.G.L. Ch. 131, § 40, and will result in impacts to Bank, Bordering
Vegetated Wetlands, and Riverfront Area. As demonstrated in the Performance Standards Analysis
prepared by Beals and Thomas submitted with the Notice of Intent, the project has been designed to
comply with the performance standards set forth under 310 CMR 10.54, 10.55, 10.58(4) and will not
have a significant or cumulative adverse effects on the resource areas. Furthermore, the targeted
herbicide treatment to control invasive phragmites will improve vegetative diversity and wildlife habitat
value.
C. The work described is within Areas Subject to Protection under the Town of Hingham Wetlands
Protection Bylaw (Article 22) including Bank, Bordering Vegetated Wetlands, Riverfront Area and Buffer
Zone and the Commission finds the areas are significant to the following wetland values: protection of
public or private water supply, protection of groundwater, flood control, erosion and sedimentation
control, storm damage prevention including coastal storm flowage, prevention of water pollution,
protection of fisheries, protection of shellfish, protection of wildlife and wildlife habitat, protection of
rare species habitat, protection of recreation and open space, protection of aesthetics.
D. As demonstrated in the Supplemental Narrative prepared by Beals and Thomas dated October 18,
2024, the project has been designed to comply with the performance standards set forth under the
Hingham Wetland Regulations (HWR) Sections 19.2, 19.3, 21.1, and will not result in an adverse effect
upon the wetland values of the resource areas. Additionally the proposed work has been found to
comply with the performance standards for work in the Buffer Zone, HWR Section 22.0(d).
E. With incorporation of the special conditions included in this Order, the Commission has determined
the project complies with the Massachusetts Wetlands Protection Act, M.G.L. Ch. 131 §40 and
Implementing Regulations, 310 CMR 10.00, and the Hingham Wetlands Protection Bylaw and Wetland
Regulations.
Suggested Special Conditions
23. Management of Common Reed (Phragmites australis) shall comply with the approved Invasive
Species Management Plan prepared by Beals and Thomas dated September 19, 2024 and Supplemental
Memorandum prepared by Beals and Thomas dated October 18, 2024 including Table 1: Protocol for
Phragmites Treatment. Any changes to the treatment methods or targeted locations as identified in the
approved Management Plan shall require review and approval of the Conservation Commission prior to
implementation.
24. Prior to commencement of invasive species management work, the applicant shall submit: final
selected herbicide EPA product labels, copy of required license(s) for all herbicide applicators, and the
BRP WM04 License to Apply Herbicides, to the Conservation Office.
25. Phragmites cut material shall be removed in select areas (i.e. open water, stream) if recommended
by the Licensed Herbicide Applicator and wetlands professional. Other cut material is permitted to
remain in place to naturally decompose.

26. Annual reports on the Invasive Species Management Plan prepared by the Licensed Aquatic
Herbicide Applicator (LHA) and/or other qualified professional shall be submitted to the Conservation
Commission detailing methods used (including dates, photos and descriptions of area(s) treated, specific
herbicides used) and results (cover of invasive species) throughout the three (3) year project. The annual
reports shall be submitted no later than December 31st of each year with the first report being
submitted after initial treatment scheduled for September or October 2025. If continued management
of phragmites is recommended by the LHA beyond the 3 year period to achieve restoration goals, an
extension of the OOC shall be requested in accordance with 310 CMR 10.05(8).
27. Upon completion of invasive species management program and prior to issuance of a Certificate of
Compliance, a final report shall be submitted to the Conservation Commission documenting overall
success of invasive species management efforts, including site photos, sketches, etc. of each treatment
area. If, based on results of treatment efforts, revegetation of any resource areas is needed to establish
a native plant community, recommendations shall be provided in the final report.
In Favor: Carolyn Nielsen, Bob Mosher, Tom Roby, Nina Villanova and Laurie Freeman
Opposed: None

Suggested Conditions of Approval

1) Erosion and sediment controls shall be installed and inspected by an agent of the Commission prior to
commencement of work; straw wattles and/or hay bales shall not be used. Sediment control devices

2) Under no conditions shall operation of equipment, storage of materials, or other site disturbance take
place on the wetland side of the limit of work line/erosion control line. Additionally, no vehicle or other
machinery refueling, lubrication, or maintenance shall take place within 100 feet of any resource area.

Opposed: None

Recommended Findings of Fact
A. The work described is within an Area Subject to Regulation under the Wetlands Protection Act, M.G.L.
Ch. 131, § 40, (Buffer Zone to Bordering Vegetated Wetlands) and with incorporation of the special
conditions included in this Order, will not alter or result in adverse impacts to the adjacent Wetland

B. The work described is within an Area Subject to Protection under the Town of Hingham Wetland
Regulations, Section 22.0 (Buffer Zone), and the Commission finds the area is significant to the following
wetland values: protection of public or private water supply, protection of groundwater, flood control,

erosion and sedimentation control, storm damage prevention, prevention of water pollution, protection
of fisheries, protection of wildlife and wildlife habitat, protection of rare species habitat, protection of
recreation and protection of aesthetics.
C. With incorporation of the special conditions included in this Order, including stormwater infiltration
and buffer zone mitigation, the proposed work has been found to comply with the performance
standards set forth under Section 22.0(d) of the Hingham Wetland Regulations and will not alter or
adversely affect the adjacent Resource Area.
D. The Commission has determined the project complies with the Massachusetts Wetlands Protection
Act, M.G.L. Ch. 131 §40 and Implementing Regulations, 310 CMR 10.00, and the Hingham Wetlands
Protection Bylaw (Article 22) and Wetland Regulations.
Suggested Special Conditions
23. The approved limit of work/sediment control line shall be staked out in the field by a registered
professional engineer or land surveyor prior to installation. The request for Pre-Construction
Meeting/Sediment Control Inspection, as required by Standard Condition #3, shall also include a
statement from the registered Professional Engineer or Professional Land Surveyor certifying that the
limit of work/sediment controls have been located and installed in accordance with the approved Site
Plan dated revised October 28, 2024 prepared by Merrill Engineers and Land Surveyors and stamped by
Brendan Sullivan, PE. The limits of the Buffer Zone Mitigation Area shall also be staked out for inspection
by the Conservation Officer.
24. The Buffer Zone Mitigation Area (370 SF) and tree mitigation (2 trees) shall be installed as shown on
the approved Site Plan dated revised October 28, 2024 prepared by Merrill Engineers and Land
Surveyors and stamped by Brendan Sullivan, PE. Any changes to the plant selections or quantities shall
be submitted to Conservation for review and approval prior to installation. Planting of the mitigation
area shall be prioritized and installed during the first growing season (April 7- November 7) following
issuance of this Order, as practical, to allow for the required two growing season survival requirement
(special condition #29).
25. Upon installation of the mitigation area, the applicant shall notify the Conservation office in writing
and include specific information on the installation date(s), plant species, quantity and size of plants,
and seed mix installed, as applicable.
26. All mitigation plantings shall be native species; no cultivars, non-native species, or invasive species
shall be allowed. Following planting, the Mitigation Area shall be allowed to naturally revegetate with
native species and remain as a naturally vegetated buffer to the adjacent resource area. Mitigation
areas shall not be disturbed, mowed or maintained as a landscaped area. This condition shall apply in
perpetuity and shall not expire with the issuance of a Certificate of Compliance.
27. Prior to the issuance of a Certificate of Compliance, the mitigation area plantings shall survive at
least two full growing seasons, unless otherwise approved by the Commission, with a minimum of 75%
survival rate. If a 75% survival rate is not achieved, replacement plantings of the same species, or
equivalent to be approved by the Conservation Officer, shall be made by the applicant. A Partial
Certificate of Compliance (if requested by the applicant) will only be considered if the mitigation area
has been planted and seeded in accordance with the approved plan.
28. After completion of work and prior to the issuance of a Certificate of Compliance, the applicant shall
permanently mark the Mitigation Area referenced in special condition #24 to ensure no inadvertent
encroachment into the area. The markers shall be installed in coordination with the Conservation Officer
and shall remain in place in perpetuity.
29. The stormwater control measures in the Buffer Zone (gravel trench and subsurface infiltration
system) shall be installed as specified on approved Site Plan dated revised October 28, 2024 prepared by
Merrill Engineers and Land Surveyors and stamped by Brendan Sullivan, PE. Documentation, including

photographs and an affidavit from a qualified individual, shall be submitted to the Conservation
Commission upon completion of installation and/or with the Request for a Certificate of Compliance.
30. It is the sole responsibility of the owner of record, Falconeiri Construction, or any successors or
assigns, to maintain the stormwater control measures (gravel trench and subsurface infiltration area) at
all times in accordance with the Long Term Pollution Prevention Plan/Operation and Maintenance Plan
prepared by Merrill Engineers and Land Surveyors dated October 28, 2024. The property owner is also
responsible for retaining records of the maintenance for review by the Commission, upon request. This
condition shall apply in perpetuity and shall not expire with the issuance of a Certificate of Compliance.
31. Upon completion of construction and prior to issuance of a Certificate of Compliance, the Applicant
shall submit to the Conservation Commission a Final As-Built Plan stamped by a Professional Land
Surveyor licensed in the Commonwealth of Massachusetts and a certification letter stamped by a
Professional Civil Engineer licensed in the Commonwealth of Massachusetts stating that the work has
been built in “substantial compliance” with the plans approved by the Conservation Commission (to
include stone trench and grass paver turn around). All deviations from the approved plans must be
noted in the letter. The As-Built Plan shall include at a minimum:
a) All wetland resource area boundaries with associated buffer zones;

Conditions for Union Street, DEP No. 034-1506, with Findings of Fact A through F and Special Conditions
23-30 as noted in the Staff Memo.
Findings of Fact
A. The Commission has found the project qualifies as a Limited Project under 310 CMR 10.53(i) “the
maintenance, repair and improvement (but not substantial enlargement except when necessary
to meet the Massachusetts Stream Crossing Standards) of structures, including dams and
reservoirs and appurtenant works to such dams and reservoirs, buildings, piers, towers, headwalls,
bridges, and culverts which existed on the effective date of April 1, 1983,” and 310 CMR 10.53(k):
“the routine maintenance and repair of road drainage structures including culverts and catch
basins, drainage easements, ditches, watercourses and artificial water conveyances to ensure flow
capacities which existed on the effective date of April 1, 1983.”
B. The Commission has found the culvert replacement project has been designed to meet the
Massachusetts Stream Crossing Standards and will improve conditions in the Aaron River for
movement of aquatic organisms and wildlife species.
C. The work described in the Notice of Intent is within Areas Subject to Protection under the
Wetlands Protection Act, M.G.L. Ch. 131, § 40, and will result in impacts to permanent impacts to
Bank, Bordering Vegetated Wetlands, BLSF, Land Under Waterbodies and Riverfront Area. As
demonstrated in the Performance Standards Analysis prepared by AECOM submitted with the
revised Notice of Intent dated October 29, 2024, the project has been designed to comply with the
standards set forth under 310 CMR 10.54, 10.55, 10.56, 10.57, and 10.58(5) and the work will not
have a significant or cumulative adverse effects on the resource areas.
D. The work described is within Areas Subject to Protection under the Town of Hingham Wetlands
Protection Bylaw (Article 22) and will result in permanent impacts to Bank, Bordering Vegetated
Wetlands, BLSF, Land Under Waterbodies, Riverfront Area and Buffer Zone and the Commission
finds the areas are significant to the following wetland values: protection of public or private water
supply, protection of groundwater, flood control, erosion and sedimentation control, storm damage
prevention including coastal storm flowage, prevention of water pollution, protection of fisheries,
protection of shellfish, protection of wildlife and wildlife habitat, protection of rare species habitat,
protection of recreation and open space, protection of aesthetics.
E. As demonstrated in the revised NOI Narrative prepared by AECOM dated October 29, 2024, the
project has been designed to comply with the performance standards set forth under the Hingham
Wetland Regulations (HWR) Sections 17.3, 19.1, 19.2, 19.3, 21.1, and will not result in an adverse
effect upon the wetland values of the resource areas. The project includes restoration of
temporarily disturbed areas and replication of BVW to mitigate for the permanent loss of wetlands
resulting from the culvert replacement. Additionally the proposed work has been found to comply
with the performance standards for work in the Buffer Zone, HWR Section 22.0(d).
F. With incorporation of the special conditions included in this Order, the Commission has determined
the project complies with the Massachusetts Wetlands Protection Act, M.G.L. Ch. 131 §40 and
Implementing Regulations, 310 CMR 10.00, and the Hingham Wetlands Protection Bylaw and
Wetland Regulations.
Recommended Special Conditions
23. Prior to commencement or work/at the pre-construction meeting referenced in Hingham Standard
Condition #3, the applicant shall submit a final construction sequence and dewatering plan as applicable
to the Conservation office.
3|Page

24. Best Management Practices (BMPs) and procedures shall be implemented within jurisdictional areas in
accordance with the revised Notice of Intent Narrative (Section 5.1) and Sheet 6 of the approved
project plans prepared by AECOM dated revised October 29, 2024 including but not limited to:
sediment and erosion control; construction access; vehicle and equipment refueling and maintenance;
material stockpiling; dewatering; pollution control measures, and restoration of disturbed areas.
25. Construction period monitoring reports shall be submitted to the Commission on a weekly basis during
construction documenting compliance with the approved plans and this Order of Conditions. The
monitoring reports shall include at a minimum: status of work in wetland areas; status of erosion and
sediment controls and BMPs including any repairs; rainfall amounts; and comments.
26. The replication for Bordering Vegetated Wetland (BVW) shall be performed in accordance with
Section 6.0 of the NOI Narrative and the Wetland Replication Plan (Sheet 6) of the approved plans
prepared by AECOM dated revised October 29, 2024. The project will replicate 73 square feet of
BVW. The Commission reserves the right to require additional seeding/plantings to ensure
achievement of 75% cover of wetland plant species within two full growing seasons, as specified in
310 CMR 10.55 (4)(b).
27. Replication construction activities must be supervised by a qualified professional, who shall be a
professional with experience in wetland replication, wetland hydrology and a working knowledge of
botany. Such a person shall be retained by the applicant to supervise and monitor construction of
the wetland replication areas until the replication area meets the requirements of this Order of
Conditions.
28. Seasonal monitoring reports shall be prepared by the qualified professional for the wetland
replication area for two growing seasons following construction. The reports shall be submitted to
the Commission by December 1st following the growing season. Monitoring reports shall describe,
using narratives, plans, and color photographs, the physical characteristics of the wetland
replication areas with respect to stability, soil characteristics, survival of vegetation and plant
mortality, aerial extent and distribution, species diversity, invasive species, etc. If after two growing
seasons, the replication area has not successfully established the required 75% yield, a contingency
plan including extended monitoring shall be submitted to the Commission for approval.
29. Areas of temporary resource area disturbance (BVW, Riverfront Area, Bank) shall be restored to
their natural condition (pre-construction elevations and conditions) following construction.
Disturbed areas within BVW shall be reseeded with NE Wetland Mix and disturbed areas within the
Riverfront Area shall be seeded with NE Roadside Upland Seed Mix or equivalent as specified in
Section 4.2 of the NOI Narrative. Reporting on the restoration of BVW shall be included in the
seasonal monitoring reports referenced in condition #27 as applicable.
30. Upon completion of construction and prior to issuance of a Certificate of Compliance, the Applicant
shall submit to the Conservation Commission a final topographical As-Built Plan stamped by a
Professional Land Surveyor licensed in the Commonwealth of Massachusetts and a certification
letter stamped by a Professional Civil Engineer licensed in the Commonwealth of Massachusetts
stating that the site work has been built in “substantial compliance” with the plans approved by the
Conservation Commission and listing all deviations, as applicable. The letter and/or plan shall
document final compensatory storage volumes and certify that no fill occurred within Bordering
Land Subject to Flooding resulting in an incremental loss of flood storage volume. The As-Built Plan
shall include:
• All wetland resource area boundaries with associated buffer zones;
• Culvert dimensions and invert elevations at inlet and outlet;
• Bottom substrate within crossing;
• Wetland replication area.
The motion passed by a roll call vote 5-0.

Thomas Tremblay, Merrill Engineers and Land Surveyors, Project Representative, updated the
Commission on the changes to the project since the last hearing. The permeable stone patio was

CO Shannon Palmer stated after the last hearing the staff comments were addressed by the engineer

discussion at the previous hearing was regarding the proposed house being constructed on a crawl
space foundation with flood vents as opposed to pilings and if the proposal met the requirements of the

meet the requirement for LSCSF as the residence will be smaller, flood resistant, and is not located in a
VE Zone or coastal A Zone. Also, the proposal will remove impervious area for an overall improvement
to the resource area. The proposed flood vents would make the residence flood resistant and allow
flood water to pass through. Ms. Palmer did voice concerns about the patio as it is proposed extremely
close to the wetland boundary. Ms. Palmer, at the Commission’s request sent a list of similar dwellings
that were previously approved in the AE zone. All examples found were on the harbor, some were in the
VE zone, and most were on pilings that were being replaced or increasing the size of the residence.
Commissioner Nielsen asked how flooding and water flow would be handled in the garage which is on a

Conditions for Union Street, DEP No. 034-1506, with Findings of Fact A through F and Special Conditions
23-30 as noted in the Staff Memo.
Findings of Fact
A. The Commission has found the project qualifies as a Limited Project under 310 CMR 10.53(i) “the
maintenance, repair and improvement (but not substantial enlargement except when necessary
to meet the Massachusetts Stream Crossing Standards) of structures, including dams and
reservoirs and appurtenant works to such dams and reservoirs, buildings, piers, towers, headwalls,
bridges, and culverts which existed on the effective date of April 1, 1983,” and 310 CMR 10.53(k):
“the routine maintenance and repair of road drainage structures including culverts and catch
basins, drainage easements, ditches, watercourses and artificial water conveyances to ensure flow
capacities which existed on the effective date of April 1, 1983.”
B. The Commission has found the culvert replacement project has been designed to meet the
Massachusetts Stream Crossing Standards and will improve conditions in the Aaron River for
movement of aquatic organisms and wildlife species.
C. The work described in the Notice of Intent is within Areas Subject to Protection under the
Wetlands Protection Act, M.G.L. Ch. 131, § 40, and will result in impacts to permanent impacts to
Bank, Bordering Vegetated Wetlands, BLSF, Land Under Waterbodies and Riverfront Area. As
demonstrated in the Performance Standards Analysis prepared by AECOM submitted with the
revised Notice of Intent dated October 29, 2024, the project has been designed to comply with the
standards set forth under 310 CMR 10.54, 10.55, 10.56, 10.57, and 10.58(5) and the work will not
have a significant or cumulative adverse effects on the resource areas.
D. The work described is within Areas Subject to Protection under the Town of Hingham Wetlands
Protection Bylaw (Article 22) and will result in permanent impacts to Bank, Bordering Vegetated
Wetlands, BLSF, Land Under Waterbodies, Riverfront Area and Buffer Zone and the Commission
finds the areas are significant to the following wetland values: protection of public or private water
supply, protection of groundwater, flood control, erosion and sedimentation control, storm damage
prevention including coastal storm flowage, prevention of water pollution, protection of fisheries,
protection of shellfish, protection of wildlife and wildlife habitat, protection of rare species habitat,
protection of recreation and open space, protection of aesthetics.
E. As demonstrated in the revised NOI Narrative prepared by AECOM dated October 29, 2024, the
project has been designed to comply with the performance standards set forth under the Hingham
Wetland Regulations (HWR) Sections 17.3, 19.1, 19.2, 19.3, 21.1, and will not result in an adverse
effect upon the wetland values of the resource areas. The project includes restoration of
temporarily disturbed areas and replication of BVW to mitigate for the permanent loss of wetlands
resulting from the culvert replacement. Additionally the proposed work has been found to comply
with the performance standards for work in the Buffer Zone, HWR Section 22.0(d).
F. With incorporation of the special conditions included in this Order, the Commission has determined
the project complies with the Massachusetts Wetlands Protection Act, M.G.L. Ch. 131 §40 and
Implementing Regulations, 310 CMR 10.00, and the Hingham Wetlands Protection Bylaw and
Wetland Regulations.
Recommended Special Conditions
23. Prior to commencement or work/at the pre-construction meeting referenced in Hingham Standard
Condition #3, the applicant shall submit a final construction sequence and dewatering plan as applicable
to the Conservation office.
3|Page

24. Best Management Practices (BMPs) and procedures shall be implemented within jurisdictional areas in
accordance with the revised Notice of Intent Narrative (Section 5.1) and Sheet 6 of the approved
project plans prepared by AECOM dated revised October 29, 2024 including but not limited to:
sediment and erosion control; construction access; vehicle and equipment refueling and maintenance;
material stockpiling; dewatering; pollution control measures, and restoration of disturbed areas.
25. Construction period monitoring reports shall be submitted to the Commission on a weekly basis during
construction documenting compliance with the approved plans and this Order of Conditions. The
monitoring reports shall include at a minimum: status of work in wetland areas; status of erosion and
sediment controls and BMPs including any repairs; rainfall amounts; and comments.
26. The replication for Bordering Vegetated Wetland (BVW) shall be performed in accordance with
Section 6.0 of the NOI Narrative and the Wetland Replication Plan (Sheet 6) of the approved plans
prepared by AECOM dated revised October 29, 2024. The project will replicate 73 square feet of
BVW. The Commission reserves the right to require additional seeding/plantings to ensure
achievement of 75% cover of wetland plant species within two full growing seasons, as specified in
310 CMR 10.55 (4)(b).
27. Replication construction activities must be supervised by a qualified professional, who shall be a
professional with experience in wetland replication, wetland hydrology and a working knowledge of
botany. Such a person shall be retained by the applicant to supervise and monitor construction of
the wetland replication areas until the replication area meets the requirements of this Order of
Conditions.
28. Seasonal monitoring reports shall be prepared by the qualified professional for the wetland
replication area for two growing seasons following construction. The reports shall be submitted to
the Commission by December 1st following the growing season. Monitoring reports shall describe,
using narratives, plans, and color photographs, the physical characteristics of the wetland
replication areas with respect to stability, soil characteristics, survival of vegetation and plant
mortality, aerial extent and distribution, species diversity, invasive species, etc. If after two growing
seasons, the replication area has not successfully established the required 75% yield, a contingency
plan including extended monitoring shall be submitted to the Commission for approval.
29. Areas of temporary resource area disturbance (BVW, Riverfront Area, Bank) shall be restored to
their natural condition (pre-construction elevations and conditions) following construction.
Disturbed areas within BVW shall be reseeded with NE Wetland Mix and disturbed areas within the
Riverfront Area shall be seeded with NE Roadside Upland Seed Mix or equivalent as specified in
Section 4.2 of the NOI Narrative. Reporting on the restoration of BVW shall be included in the
seasonal monitoring reports referenced in condition #27 as applicable.
30. Upon completion of construction and prior to issuance of a Certificate of Compliance, the Applicant
shall submit to the Conservation Commission a final topographical As-Built Plan stamped by a
Professional Land Surveyor licensed in the Commonwealth of Massachusetts and a certification
letter stamped by a Professional Civil Engineer licensed in the Commonwealth of Massachusetts
stating that the site work has been built in “substantial compliance” with the plans approved by the
Conservation Commission and listing all deviations, as applicable. The letter and/or plan shall
document final compensatory storage volumes and certify that no fill occurred within Bordering
Land Subject to Flooding resulting in an incremental loss of flood storage volume. The As-Built Plan
shall include:
• All wetland resource area boundaries with associated buffer zones;
• Culvert dimensions and invert elevations at inlet and outlet;
• Bottom substrate within crossing;
• Wetland replication area.

Findings of Fact
A. The work described is within Areas Subject to Protection under the Town of Hingham Wetland
Regulations 22.0 (Buffer Zone), and the Commission finds the areas are significant to the following
wetland values: protection of public or private water supply, protection of groundwater, flood

Suggested Conditions of Approval

3. Vote to issue Order of Conditions, Union Street Wompatuck Park, DEP No. 034-1506
The hearing was closed at the November 4, 2024 meeting. Staff reviewed recommended conditions.
Vote: Commissioner Freeman made a motion, seconded by Commissioner Mosher, to issue an Order of
Conditions for Union Street, DEP No. 034-1506, with Findings of Fact A through F and Special Conditions
23-30 as noted in the Staff Memo.
Findings of Fact
A. The Commission has found the project qualifies as a Limited Project under 310 CMR 10.53(i) “the
maintenance, repair and improvement (but not substantial enlargement except when necessary
to meet the Massachusetts Stream Crossing Standards) of structures, including dams and
reservoirs and appurtenant works to such dams and reservoirs, buildings, piers, towers, headwalls,
bridges, and culverts which existed on the effective date of April 1, 1983,” and 310 CMR 10.53(k):
“the routine maintenance and repair of road drainage structures including culverts and catch
basins, drainage easements, ditches, watercourses and artificial water conveyances to ensure flow
capacities which existed on the effective date of April 1, 1983.”
B. The Commission has found the culvert replacement project has been designed to meet the
Massachusetts Stream Crossing Standards and will improve conditions in the Aaron River for
movement of aquatic organisms and wildlife species.
C. The work described in the Notice of Intent is within Areas Subject to Protection under the
Wetlands Protection Act, M.G.L. Ch. 131, § 40, and will result in impacts to permanent impacts to
Bank, Bordering Vegetated Wetlands, BLSF, Land Under Waterbodies and Riverfront Area. As
demonstrated in the Performance Standards Analysis prepared by AECOM submitted with the
revised Notice of Intent dated October 29, 2024, the project has been designed to comply with the
standards set forth under 310 CMR 10.54, 10.55, 10.56, 10.57, and 10.58(5) and the work will not
have a significant or cumulative adverse effects on the resource areas.
D. The work described is within Areas Subject to Protection under the Town of Hingham Wetlands
Protection Bylaw (Article 22) and will result in permanent impacts to Bank, Bordering Vegetated
Wetlands, BLSF, Land Under Waterbodies, Riverfront Area and Buffer Zone and the Commission
finds the areas are significant to the following wetland values: protection of public or private water
supply, protection of groundwater, flood control, erosion and sedimentation control, storm damage
prevention including coastal storm flowage, prevention of water pollution, protection of fisheries,
protection of shellfish, protection of wildlife and wildlife habitat, protection of rare species habitat,
protection of recreation and open space, protection of aesthetics.
E. As demonstrated in the revised NOI Narrative prepared by AECOM dated October 29, 2024, the
project has been designed to comply with the performance standards set forth under the Hingham
Wetland Regulations (HWR) Sections 17.3, 19.1, 19.2, 19.3, 21.1, and will not result in an adverse
effect upon the wetland values of the resource areas. The project includes restoration of
temporarily disturbed areas and replication of BVW to mitigate for the permanent loss of wetlands
resulting from the culvert replacement. Additionally the proposed work has been found to comply
with the performance standards for work in the Buffer Zone, HWR Section 22.0(d).
F. With incorporation of the special conditions included in this Order, the Commission has determined
the project complies with the Massachusetts Wetlands Protection Act, M.G.L. Ch. 131 §40 and
Implementing Regulations, 310 CMR 10.00, and the Hingham Wetlands Protection Bylaw and
Wetland Regulations.
Recommended Special Conditions
23. Prior to commencement or work/at the pre-construction meeting referenced in Hingham Standard
Condition #3, the applicant shall submit a final construction sequence and dewatering plan as applicable
to the Conservation office.
3|Page

24. Best Management Practices (BMPs) and procedures shall be implemented within jurisdictional areas in
accordance with the revised Notice of Intent Narrative (Section 5.1) and Sheet 6 of the approved
project plans prepared by AECOM dated revised October 29, 2024 including but not limited to:
sediment and erosion control; construction access; vehicle and equipment refueling and maintenance;
material stockpiling; dewatering; pollution control measures, and restoration of disturbed areas.
25. Construction period monitoring reports shall be submitted to the Commission on a weekly basis during
construction documenting compliance with the approved plans and this Order of Conditions. The
monitoring reports shall include at a minimum: status of work in wetland areas; status of erosion and
sediment controls and BMPs including any repairs; rainfall amounts; and comments.
26. The replication for Bordering Vegetated Wetland (BVW) shall be performed in accordance with
Section 6.0 of the NOI Narrative and the Wetland Replication Plan (Sheet 6) of the approved plans
prepared by AECOM dated revised October 29, 2024. The project will replicate 73 square feet of
BVW. The Commission reserves the right to require additional seeding/plantings to ensure
achievement of 75% cover of wetland plant species within two full growing seasons, as specified in
310 CMR 10.55 (4)(b).
27. Replication construction activities must be supervised by a qualified professional, who shall be a
professional with experience in wetland replication, wetland hydrology and a working knowledge of
botany. Such a person shall be retained by the applicant to supervise and monitor construction of
the wetland replication areas until the replication area meets the requirements of this Order of
Conditions.
28. Seasonal monitoring reports shall be prepared by the qualified professional for the wetland
replication area for two growing seasons following construction. The reports shall be submitted to
the Commission by December 1st following the growing season. Monitoring reports shall describe,
using narratives, plans, and color photographs, the physical characteristics of the wetland
replication areas with respect to stability, soil characteristics, survival of vegetation and plant
mortality, aerial extent and distribution, species diversity, invasive species, etc. If after two growing
seasons, the replication area has not successfully established the required 75% yield, a contingency
plan including extended monitoring shall be submitted to the Commission for approval.
29. Areas of temporary resource area disturbance (BVW, Riverfront Area, Bank) shall be restored to
their natural condition (pre-construction elevations and conditions) following construction.
Disturbed areas within BVW shall be reseeded with NE Wetland Mix and disturbed areas within the
Riverfront Area shall be seeded with NE Roadside Upland Seed Mix or equivalent as specified in
Section 4.2 of the NOI Narrative. Reporting on the restoration of BVW shall be included in the
seasonal monitoring reports referenced in condition #27 as applicable.
30. Upon completion of construction and prior to issuance of a Certificate of Compliance, the Applicant
shall submit to the Conservation Commission a final topographical As-Built Plan stamped by a
Professional Land Surveyor licensed in the Commonwealth of Massachusetts and a certification
letter stamped by a Professional Civil Engineer licensed in the Commonwealth of Massachusetts
stating that the site work has been built in “substantial compliance” with the plans approved by the
Conservation Commission and listing all deviations, as applicable. The letter and/or plan shall
document final compensatory storage volumes and certify that no fill occurred within Bordering
Land Subject to Flooding resulting in an incremental loss of flood storage volume. The As-Built Plan
shall include:
• All wetland resource area boundaries with associated buffer zones;
• Culvert dimensions and invert elevations at inlet and outlet;
• Bottom substrate within crossing;
• Wetland replication area.
The motion passed by a roll call vote 5-0.

Walter Sullivan, Esq., representing the applicant, advised the Commission that some changes have been
made to the plans based on comments made at the last hearing which Brendan Sullivan, PE, of Merrill
Engineers will review. A waiver will no longer be requested as the stormwater had been modified.
Brendan Sullivan, PE, Merrill Engineers, reviewed the plan revisions with the Commission: two, 6 inch
perforated pipes were added in the shoulder of the driveway which would be in 2 foot x 2 foot of
crushed stone to catch run off; the rain garden (which had been designed for extreme rain events using
Cornell numbers) was made bigger for peak flow so less water now flows toward Rockland St. post
11 | P a g e

construction; the first 40-50’ of the driveway is proposed to be pervious; and 600 sq. ft. was added to
the plan for mitigation plantings with salt tolerant species.
CO Shannon Palmer stated at this time the representative has addressed the Commissions comments
regarding the paved portion of the driveway within LSCSF, expanding the rain garden, and adding the
pipe to manage run off. Ms. Palmer spoke to the fact that the encroachment in the 50’ buffer can be
allowed considering that there is a state highway in between the now pervious portion of the driveway
and the resource area. She commented there would still be a paved, steep driveway within the
Commissions jurisdiction and that maintenance of the rain garden will be critical to reducing long term
impacts from runoff and flooding to the resource area. The CO also noted the application has not been
through planning for stormwater review and there have not been any test pits done in the area of rain
garden. She suggested the Commission deliberate on if the proposed activity would cause detrimental
impacts to the resource area from flooding or pollution triggered by a storm event.
Commissioner Hidell asked how the lower part of the driveway would be treated.
B. Sullivan replied it would be a solid surface such as pervious paver or pavement. There was a proposed
trench drain at the end of the driveway so gravel would not be possible.
Commissioner Nielsen commented that the driveway was very steep. Ms. Nielsen expressed concerns
with how the driveway would be treated and mentioned sodium chloride would not be a good option
due to the proximity to the ACEC. Sand would also not be a good option as it could wash into the trench
drain at the bottom of the driveway and potentially ending up in the rain garden.
B. Sullivan commented that an environmental friendly deicing solvent could potentially be found. Mr.
Sullivan didn’t think deicing chemicals for the driveway would add much of a consequence to what is
already used in the area.
Mr. Hidell asked what the percentage of slope was in the lower section of the driveway.
B. Sullivan replied that it was 23-24% of a slope.
Ms. Nielsen expressed concern over the rain garden being critical to the functioning of the drainage of
the steep driveway. Ms. Nielsen wanted to know how it would be ensured that the rain garden stays
maintained long term.
B. Sullivan suggested putting the maintenance of the rain garden in the conditions. He agreed that the
maintenance is important to function properly. He advised that the plan still has to go through planning
to be approved.
Ms. Nielsen and Mr. Hidell suggested that peer review through planning for stormwater should be done
before the Commission moves ahead with the project.
B. Sullivan advised that the project has not been submitted to planning at this time.
There was discussion among W. Sullivan and B. Sullivan with the Commission of putting conditions on
the project so it can move ahead to planning.
Ms. Nielsen expressed she did not feel comfortable moving ahead without seeing the stormwater
report.

12 | P a g e

Mr. Hidell also voiced concern about not having sufficient information to move forward including the
test pits in the area of the rain garden. He noted the rain garden is critical to manage the flow of water.
Marybeth White, 218 Hull St, was happy to see that the rain garden had been expanded. She
commented that just a couple days prior with the full moon tide right at 311 Rockland St the tide had
come up and crossed over the road onto this property. Ms. White asked what would happen to the rain
garden when the marsh over flows.
B. Sullivan advised that salt tolerant plants will be planted and able to withstand water from the river.
Ms. White is concerned that when there is a rain event and flooding event that the rain garden won’t be
enough to take on all of the water.
B. Sullivan advised that the road elevation is at a 7 or 8, and the 100 year rain storm could come up over
10, so Rockland St could be under 2’ of water.
Ms. White commented that the flooding happens on at least a yearly basis not every 100 years. This past
week it was just a full moon without rain that flooded the road.
B. Sullivan commented that run off from the site will be mitigated through the rain garden and it has
been shown that there will be less flow going to Rockland St post construction than pre construction.
Ms. White commented that she is concerned that the very steep driveway will create a waterfall of
water to make the flooding worse.
No other members of the public commented on the application.
After discussion, the applicant agreed to the continuance to allow for peer review of the stormwater.
Vote: Commissioner Mosher made a motion, seconded by Commissioner Hidell, to continue the public
hearing for 311 Rockland Street, DEP No. 034-1501 to December 16, 2024. The motion passed by a roll
call vote 5-0.
In Favor: Carolyn Nielsen, Bob Mosher, Bob Hidell, Nina Villanova and Laurie Freeman
Recused: Thomas Roby
Opposed: None
4. Notice of Intent, 55 Industrial Park Road, DEP No. 034-15XX, Fifty-Five Saxon Hingham, LLC
Proof of Abutter Notification including an Affidavit of Service was submitted to the Conservation office.
Phil Cordeiro, Allen and Major Associates, Project Representative, gave an overview of the project.
Proposed is demolition of two commercial buildings on site and construction of a two story office
building and improving the site. The driveway and parking area will be reused. The new building would
be further away from the resource area. The new building is proposed to be further away from the
riverfront. Stormwater management is proposed to be improved. Resource areas include Riverfront
Area and Buffer Zone to Bordering Vegetated Wetland associated with a pond. There is a potential
vernal pool at the rear of the property which will be studied in the spring. Mr. Cordeiro explained since
the application was prepared, the flood maps were updated and there is no longer flood zone on the
property. The proposal also includes removal of numerous trees that have been identified by a certified
arborist as being dead or diseased.

13 | P a g e

Sean Papich, Sean Papich Landscape Design, went over the landscape design proposal. The proposal
reflected many native and natural plants along the property.
CO Shannon Palmer noted the revised plans presented at the meeting had not been submitted for
review. Once plans are reviewed staff will provide comments and recommendations for the next
hearing.
No members of the public commented on the application. No DEP file received.
Vote: Commissioner Villanova made a motion, seconded by Commissioner Mosher, to continue the
public hearing for 55 Industrial Park Rd, with consent of applicant, to December 16, 2024 at 7PM. The
motion passed by a roll call vote 6-0.
In Favor: Carolyn Nielsen, Bob Mosher, Bob Hidell, Tom Roby, Nina Villanova and Laurie Freeman
Opposed: None
5. Notice of Intent, 6 Whiton Ave, DEP No. 034-1511, ALR Homes
Proof of Abutter Notification including an Affidavit of Service was submitted to the Conservation office.
Paul Seaberg, Grady Consulting LLC, spoke to the Commission about the proposed project for a raze and
rebuild of a single family home. The new home is designed accordance for building code within a flood
zone. The existing home is not compliant with existing flood zone requirements. The new home will
have flood vents to allow passage of water.
Shannon Palmer stated the office received revised plans earlier in the day but they have not been
reviewed.
Commissioner Nielsen asked the public to hold their comments until the Commission can review the
revised plans.
Vote: Commissioner Mosher made a motion seconded by Commissioner Freeman to continue the public
hearing for 6 Whiton Ave, DEP No. 034-1511, with consent of applicant to December 16, 2024 at 7PM.
The motion passed by a roll call vote 6-0.
In Favor: Carolyn Nielsen, Bob Mosher, Bob Hidell, Tom Roby, Nina Villanova and Laurie Freeman
Opposed: None

Shannon Palmer stated the Tranquility Grove project was withdrawn from CPC consideration. The
Bennett property application is moving forward.

## Full Document Content

Town of Hingham

HINGHAM CLIMATE ACTION COMMISSION
MEETING MINUTES
DATE: December 3, 2025
PLACE: Online via Zoom
MEMBERS PRESENT: Brad Moyer, Elliott Place, Jo-An Heileman, Lisa Hennessey, Doug Troyer, Matt
Curran, Gary Tondorf-Dick, Tom Morahan
MEMBERS ABSENT: Alyson Anderson
GUESTS: John Borger, Brianna Bennett, Brenda Black, Paul Sprecher, Patricia Burke, Anita Ryan
Opening and Call to Order: Chair Brad Moyer called the remote meeting to order at 7:03pm. He
opened the meeting with the required remote-meeting and recording notices, confirmed that the session
was being recorded in compliance with Massachusetts Open Meeting Law, and welcomed members to
the meeting.
Agenda Item 1: Climate Leaders Update: decarbonization roadmap and ZEV first policy
Brad Moyer reported that the Town submitted an application for a Technical Assistance Grant from
DOER at the end of November. As DOER prioritizes communities that meet four of the six criteria for
the Climate Leaders Program (as Hingham does), there is reason to be cautiously optimistic about our
chances of winning the grant. Doug Troyer asked for clarification on the ZEV policy. John Borger
publicly thanked the committee for their work.
Agenda Item 2: Discuss the Commonwealth’s possible pilot program expansion for banning fossil
fuels
The Commonwealth allowed up to ten communities to ban all new fossil fuel gas hookups as a pilot
program beginning in 2022. The Commonwealth is currently discussing whether to expand this
program. No decisions have been made. The question for HCAC is whether we would be interested in
promoting admissions to the pilot program should it be expanded. Questions to be considered are how
we would position ourselves for this initiative and what other initiatives we may have to put on hold
(e.g. the Zero Emission Vehicle First Policy).
1

Jo-An Heileman suggested that being such an early adopter of the pilot program may be out-of-step with
Hingham’s municipal culture and history. Maria Zade asked how such a policy would be enacted. Brad
answered that it would be a bylaw change. Maria responded that it would be good to know the
timeframe for expansion. Will there be opportunities to join the program within the next 2 – 5 years?
Paul asked how retrofits of old buildings would factor into the pilot program and the costs to the Town.
He also wondered what incentives and grants come with admission to the program.
Brenda pointed out that the ZEV policy would not need Town Meeting approval while pilot program
entry would. John Borger would like to know what the current rate of new construction gas hookups in
the Town is and whether it is more commercial or residential. That information will help us to
understand how impactful entry into this program could be.
The committee decided that it would choose members to reach out to communities that are currently in
the pilot program. Patricia Burke and Maria Zade will try to speak with officials in Lexington and Acton
about their experience and report back. Patricia will also try to reach out to other communities. John
Borger offered to speak with Zero Carbon MA, one of the proponents of the program, and report back.
Committee members and guests will report back to the full committee within the next 2-3 meetings.
Agenda Item 3: Solar net-metering/payback for residential solar installations that contribute to the
grid
Solar net-metering/payback allows HMLP to pay solar panel homeowners for excess energy produced.
As some members of the Hingham Light Board are considered “early adopters” of solar panels, voting in
favor of such a policy is seen as a conflict of interest per the State Ethics Board. The Light Board is further
restricted from setting rates that would affect less than 10% of the community, which would be the case
with setting rates for solar panel homes in Hingham. The question is how we can support adoption of
solar panels in Hingham given that the Light Board is currently restricted from offering incentives for
excess energy produced. Brad asked if the HCAC could be considered an impartial advisor whose opinion
would allow the Light Board to support this policy (or not). One option is to petition the State Ethics
Board to reconsider their decision as the policy is inadvertently punishing the Town for electing
progressive board members. Brad offered to discuss with the Light Board what role HCAC may be able
to have with petitioning the State Ethics Board.
Agenda Item 4: Opportunities for engagement on public projects
a.

Hingham Housing Authority Beal Street senior units

This is a large multiunit housing project being proposed in West Hingham. HCAC can watch and be present
at these meetings to try to ensure that the Town’s climate goals are being considered. Lisa Hennessey and
Matt Curran volunteered to keep tabs on this project. Anita Ryan (37 Baker Hill Dr) shared that there used to
be an ammunition depot at the proposed site and she hopes that the new building will follow the existing
concrete footprint and minimize disturbance of the forest. Doug Troyer pointed out the Conservation
Commission will need to give approval as there are several protected areas on the site.
b. Library HVAC replacement
2

In early November, the Select Board approved an agreement with Allied Consulting Engineering Services to
design a replacement for the town library’s failing HVAC chiller system, authorizing up to $80,000 in funding
for the engineering work. The total capital project is likely to exceed $580,000. This is another opportunity to
get in from the early stages and be sure that the Climate Action Plan is upheld. Jo-An volunteered to keep
watch on this project.

Agenda Item 5: Warrant article submission and follow-on processes
The warrant article for dissolution of the EAC and reconfiguration of the HCAC has been submitted. Next
steps are to plan socialization and an Advisory Committee presentation.
Agenda Item 6: Review and approve the minutes from the previous meeting
The minutes were approved.
Agenda Item 7: Other business brought before the Commission
John Borger shared that Hingham Net Zero is discussing adoption of heat pumps within Hingham,
especially in homes transitioning from oil. The transition rate (from all types of homes) is lower than
hoped for. HNZ is considering options to reach beyond early adopters. They are also looking at ways to
get better data about homes that are likely candidates for conversion with the goal of targeting outreach to
those homes. HCAC members discussed how we could support such an effort.
Agenda Item 8: Adjourn at 8:40 pm
Next Meeting: January 7, 2026

3

HINGHAM AFFORDABLE HOUSING TRUST
HINGHAM, MASSACHUSETTS
MEETING MINUTES

Date: September 20, 2017
Location: South Hearing Room, Hingham Town Hall
Called to Order: 7:05 pm
Attendance: Tim White, Chairman; Brittan DuBose, Anita Comerford, Nancy Kerber, Mike MacDonald,
Al Chambers, Kathleen Amonte
Approval of Minutes from Meeting of August 16, 2017: Voted – a motion was made by Kathleen
Amonte and seconded by Anita Comerford to approve the Open Session minutes from August 16, 2017.
A vote was taken and all were in favor; the motion passed.
Treasurer’s Report/Approval of Invoice: Anita went over the report. The September report will show
the $150,000 payment for Rust House. Anita and Sue Nickerson were wondering if they could account
for Lincoln School separately. Tim does not see an issue and thinks it would clarify things.
Voted – a motion was made by Nancy Kerber and seconded by Brittan DuBose to approve the NAHRO
invoice of $75. A vote was taken and all were in favor; the motion passed.
Voted – a motion was made by Al Chambers and seconded by Nancy Kerber to approve a bill from
GateHouse Media for the advertising of the RFP for Whiting Street. A vote was taken and all were in
favor; the motion passed.
Voted – a motion was made by Al Chambers and seconded by Nancy Kerber to approve a bill from
MacKenzie for 10 Cedar Street work. A vote was taken and all were in favor; the motion passed.
Voted – a motion was made by Al Chambers and seconded by Brittan DuBose to approve the treasurers
report. A vote was taken and all were in favor; the motion passed.
Whiting Street: There was one response to the RFP, Habitat for Humanity. Carol Costello was kind
enough to put together an evaluation form. Trust members took time to evaluate the proposal
individually. Before they did that, the Board agreed to skip to Beal Street for a few minutes since there
was a resident there who wanted to speak to the Trust.
80 Beal Street: Shannon Brinkley attended. She owns one of the affordable units and is concerned with
the costs that have come up. Her condo fee has doubled and she was assessed $4375 for snow removal
from two years ago. She felt there was very short notice and felt threatened to pay. Her concern is that
she will not be able to stay there. Tim does not believe there is a cap on her condo fees. The Trust finds
the fact that the condo fees have gone up so quickly troubling.
Al mentions that the condo association should consider making it a town road so the town would plow
it. Tim will follow up with the condo association before the next meeting and will also reach out to
DHCD.

HINGHAM AFFORDABLE HOUSING TRUST
HINGHAM, MASSACHUSETTS
MEETING MINUTES
Whiting Street (Resumed): Tim collects the evaluation forms and the results are tallied. The proposal is
clearly met with approval from the Trust. The next procedure is to vote and send notice to Habitat.
Then there will be a negotiation procedure and everyone will come up with a schedule. Mike had a
question on funding, which was discussed.
Voted – A motion was made by Mike MacDonald and seconded by Nancy Kerber - Will the Hingham
Affordable Housing Trust (the “Trust”) designate South Shore Habitat for Humanity (the ”Habitat”), 20
Mathewson Drive, Weymouth, MA 02189, as the Designated Developer of the property known as 302304 Whiting Street, Hingham, MA 02043, subject to certain conditions and terms outlined in the Whiting
Street Property Request for Proposals (the “RFP”), due on September 13, 2017, and the Habitat
Response to the RFP? A vote was taken and all were in favor; the motion passed.
Rust House: The purchase closed last week. A deed rider has been drafted that is the standard
affordability rider. Now Father Bill’s is working to get the property on the town’s affordability inventory.
Old Ship: Tim has been contacted by Old Ship. The developer is out of the picture. The church would
like to set up a meeting with folks from the Town and would like Tim to attend.
Selectmen’s Parcel: Nancy had a good meeting with Sharon Napier from the Hingham Housing
Authority about 100 Beal Street. They are proposing a mix of affordable apartments for 55+. Right now
there is a deed restriction on the property that prevents them from doing that which expires in March of
2018. The Housing Authority did a needs assessment study. They would like to have a local and veteran
preference. Tim and Nancy will try to attend their next meeting.
The Trust is asked to think about what they can do to maintain affordable units in Town.
Lincoln School Apartments Update: Aylene was sick and could not attend. She gave an update via
email.
On the elevator project: still some back and forth going on with the Town, the RFP should go out by end
of September for work to start in April, the Town had asked the consultant to make some changes in his
proposed RFP and all have been made.
Other improvements underway include new outdoor benches which should be in early October and also
new outdoor lights which will be done 1/2 in 2017 and 1/2 in 2018.
There is a new onsite maintenance manager in place, named Ryan, the fellow that had been there for
years retired. The residents couldn't say enough positive about the new fellow and seem to love him.
The Board asked Ryan to do a "review" of the property as a fresh set of eyes and plan a walk around
with him on 10/3 at 8 am if anyone wants to join us.

Conservation
Subject: Ensuring Responsible Stewardship of Hingham’s Natural Resources

Dear Members of the Hingham Conservation Commission,
While recreational opportunities are important, they must be balanced with the responsibility to protect Hingham’s
natural environment for stewardship and for future generations.
This proposal to build 8 pickleball courts raises concerns due to its location near wetlands that feed the already
stressed Back River, as well as its proximity to an Area of Critical Environmental Concern (ACEC). Notably, the
ACEC boundary is not clearly identified in the proposal materials, making it difficult to assess impacts.
The site also supports many migratory bird species identified by the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service, many of which
nest nearby. The noise from pickleball could disrupt these habitats, and seasonal restrictions should be required.
Encroachment into buffer zones, including within the 50-foot buffer (no matter how small) and the 200-foot Riverfront,
wastes an opportunity to provide these sensitive natural resources with the space to recover, flourish and avoid longterm environmental harm. While the reduction in impervious area is helpful, the Town should lead by adhering strictly
and demonstrating commitment to its bylaws.
The ongoing and continuously encroaching developments in the area has already impacted these wetlands. Adding
further pressure, especially at the scale of eight courts—exceeding Hingham’s typical maximum of six—raises
serious concerns.
If this project proceeds, it should include strong safeguards: no salt, fertilizer, or chemical use, and landscaping that
restores natural vegetation rather than introducing grass areas.
The decisions made today will shape the health of these ecosystems for years to come. I urge the Commission to
act with caution and prioritize environmental preservation.
Thank you for your consideration.
Sincerely,
Hilary Aborn

Conservation
Proposed Pickleball courts on Back River

Subject: Request to Modify Proposed Pickleball Courts Near Sensitive Wetlands
Dear Members of the Hingham Conservation Commission,
I am writing to respectfully urge the Commission to significantly modify the Recreation Department’s
proposal to construct eight pickleball courts in an environmentally sensitive area.
The proposal relies on a reduction in impervious surface from demolition of a former naval
ammunition structure to justify encroachment into wetland buffer zones. This tradeoff should not
come at the expense of established protections. The Town should demonstrate environmental
stewardship by fully honoring its own wetland bylaws.
The plan for 8 pickleball courts includes development within the 50-foot buffer in contravention of
Bylaw 23.2 (irrespective of how small; it still occurs), and does not adequately respect the 200-foot
Riverfront boundary. This is particularly concerning given that the river is an Outstanding Resource
Water feeding the Back River Estuary.
These wetlands support the Back River, which is already polluted and undergoing rehabilitation.
Additional encroachment will only hinder recovery. The adjacent Back River Area of Critical
Environmental Concern (ACEC), whose boundary does not seem to be clearly or accurately
demarcated in the NOI materials, underscores the ecological sensitivity of this site.
The U.S. Fish & Wildlife Serviceidentifies 23 migratory bird species in this area, many of which nest
nearby. The noise associated with pickleball raises serious concerns, and play should be prohibited
during nesting seasons.
I also urge the Commission to prohibit the use of salt, fertilizers, and chemical treatments such as
mosquito spraying, as a condition to any order due to the proximity to sensitive natural resources.
Landscaping should favor natural vegetation rather than maintained grass areas, particularly to the
north and west.
Finally, the scale of this proposal is excessive. Nowhere else in Hingham are eight courts
constructed—six courts has been the maximum and should remain the standard.
Given cumulative environmental impacts already observed in the area, including harm to wetlands
and vernal pools, this proposal warrants strong reconsideration.
Sincerely,
Steve Cobble

Conservation
Subject: Concerns Regarding Compliance with Wetland and ACEC Protections

Dear Conservation Commission,
I am writing to raise concerns regarding the 8 proposed pickleball courts and their compliance with the spirit of
Hingham’s wetland bylaws and environmental protections.
The proposal, irrespective of how small, includes development within the 50-foot buffer, which conflicts with
Bylaw 23.2, and does not appear to fully respect the 200-foot Riverfront boundary associated with an
Outstanding Resource Water.
The rationale of reduced impervious surface does not justify these encroachments. Upholding bylaw
requirements is essential to maintaining regulatory integrity.
The wetlands feed and support the Back River, an impaired system undergoing restoration. Additional
encroachment could undermine these efforts. The riverfront in the vicinity of the development is associated
with Hockley Run, which is an essential part of the ecosystem and feeds the fish run associated with the Back
River. That fish in turn are food for the many fish further out to sea on which we depend for food.
Furthermore, the project area lies adjacent to an Area of Critical Environmental Concern (ACEC), yet its
boundary is not clearly demarcated in the application materials. This lack of clarity raises concerns about
whether impacts have been fully assessed. The ACEC nomination, which was unanimously brought by the
Town’s Select Board, Planning Board, the Conservation Commission and the Bare Cove Park Committee,
referred to the many migratory birds in the area and that this habitat was worthy of the utmost protection for
wildlife. Noise impacts from pickleball are completely out of character with that protection and should be
addressed, including prohibiting play during nesting seasons.
I also advocate strict prohibitions on salt, fertilizer, and chemical use, and a requirement for naturalized
landscaping, as a condition of any development in the area.
Finally, the proposed scale of eight courts exceeds Hingham’s norm of six courts and should be reduced
accordingly.
Our founder, Mary F. Toomey, with the support of Dr. Mary Sears of the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution
worked tirelessly in the sixties and seventies to preserve the Back River and the surrounding land. It’s time for
Hingham to embrace their legacy and work to protect this valuable resource rather than destroy it.
I urge the Commission to ensure full compliance and appropriate protections.
Respectfully,
Linda DiAngelo
President, Back River Watershed Association

Dear Members of the Commission,
I am writing to respectfully express concern about the proposed pickleball courts and their impact on the
wetlands and the Back River watershed.
These wetlands directly feed the Back River, which is already polluted and undergoing rehabilitation. This
eight-pickleball court proposal encroaches into buffer zones—particularly within the 50-foot buffer and near the
200-foot Riverfront—and risks further degrading this fragile system.
The adjacent Back River Area of Critical Environmental Concern, though not clearly delineated in the Notice of
Intent, highlights the ecological importance of this area and stresses the need to fully respect the riverfront and
wetland buffers. This area is also home to many migratory bird species, many of which nest nearby. The noise
associated with pickleball could significantly disrupt these populations, warranting seasonal restrictions for the
noise, not to mention disturbing nearby human residents.
Cumulative development has already negatively impacted these wetlands and nearby vernal pool. It needs to
stop. This project’s encroachment into buffer zones, adds further risk to that harm. While the reduction in
impervious area for this development is a positive, the missed opportunity to honor these wetlands and the
protections this Town afforded them in creating wetland and riverfront buffer areas would sadly be lost
forever. For pickleball?
Additionally, and notably, nowhere has Town built eight courts for anything and this number exceeds local
precedent. This development should be reduced to six courts at most in line with other public courts built in
Hingham. Pickleball is a fad that will fade in due time, leaving us with more unsightly unused hardscape that
requires upkeep.
I urge you to consider that the health of the watershed should take priority over and be appropriately balanced
against expanded recreation. Thank you for your attention.
Sincerely,

Marisa C. Ronan

April 9, 2026

Dear Members of the Select Board and Conservation Commission,
I am writing in response to the letters and in-person concerns raised at your recent meetings
regarding the Pickleball Project approved at the 2025 Town Meeting.
Some critics have suggested that the late Mary Toomey—former Chair of the Back River
Committee of Weymouth and Hingham and a respected environmental advocate—would have
opposed this project. While Mary was deeply committed to protecting natural resources, her
vision centered on preserving the river and estuary from contamination, providing safe habitat
for wildlife, and creating parkland that is accessible to the public.
I had the privilege of knowing Mary and working alongside her in advocating for the cleanup of
Jay Cashman’s property on Route 3A in North Weymouth. At the time, the rear of that property
had become an illegal dumping ground, as documented in a Patriot Ledger article dated April
1994. Our efforts, along with those of others, ultimately contributed to the creation of Abigail
Adams State Park, which was dedicated in 2003. Mary was later honored with a plaque at the
site—a ceremony I was proud to attend as her friend and supporter.
In that spirit, I believe Mary would recognize the value of the approved pickleball project. The
Recreation Commission is taking the lead in removing the Tracers Building, a condemned
building. We will be cleaning up the site which currently has pipes, cement blocks and other
debris strewn aside it.
Importantly, the project has been designed to avoid impacts to the wetlands and the nearby
vernal pool. The engineering plans clearly outline measures to meet all environmental
requirements.
This project represents a meaningful opportunity to remove a condemned building and protect
the natural resources Mary Toomey worked so hard to preserve.
Thank you for your time, consideration, and continued service to our community.
Sincerely,
Vicki Donlan
Chair, Hingham Recreation Commission

Request to Modify Proposed Pickleball Courts Near Sensitive Wetlands

Dear Members of the Hingham Conservation Commission,
I am writing to respectfully urge the Commission to significantly modify the Recreation Department’s proposal
to construct eight pickleball courts in an environmentally sensitive area.
The proposal relies on a reduction in impervious surface from demolition of a former naval ammunition
structure to justify encroachment into wetland buffer zones. This tradeoff should not come at the expense of
established protections. The Town should demonstrate environmental stewardship by fully honoring its own
wetland bylaws.
The plan for 8 pickleball courts includes development within the 50-foot buffer in contravention of Bylaw 23.2
(irrespective of how small, encroachment still occurs), and does not adequately respect the 200-foot
Riverfront boundary. This is particularly concerning given that the river is an Outstanding Resource Water
feeding the Back River Estuary.
These wetlands support the Back River, which is already polluted and undergoing rehabilitation. Additional
encroachment will only hinder recovery. The adjacent Back River Area of Critical Environmental Concern
(ACEC), whose boundary does not seem to be clearly or accurately demarcated in the NOI materials,
underscores the ecological sensitivity of this site.
The U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service identifies 23 migratory bird species in this area, many of which nest nearby.
The noise associated with pickleball raises serious concerns, and play should be prohibited during nesting
seasons.
I also urge the Commission to prohibit the use of salt, fertilizers, and chemical treatments such as mosquito
spraying, as a condition to any order due to the proximity to sensitive natural resources. Landscaping should
favor natural vegetation rather than maintained grass areas, particularly to the north and west.
As an aside, I do not personally know of any type of mosquito spraying, no matter how friendlysounding the company name, that is not harmful to water life (if you do know of any, please pass it
along).
Finally, the scale of this proposal is excessive. Nowhere else in Hingham are eight courts constructed—six
courts has been the maximum and should remain the standard.
Given cumulative environmental impacts already observed in the area, including harm to wetlands and vernal
pools, this proposal warrants strong reconsideration.

drought, development and water diversion from its hey-day of
supplying water
for the Naval ammo depot. Nonetheless, the
swamp is still vital as the headwaters of an ecosystem (spring
water runoff from Conservatory Park and Baker's Hill, many
wetlands, and Hockley Run) that form an essential tributary to the
food-producing (alewives/river herring, a keystone species in the
marine food chain) Back River estuary, a nourishing mix of fresh
and salt water, and its river herring run, one of the largest in the
state.

An initial study completed in May 2024 was developed to determine the best
location for the pickleball courts. Seven (7) sites were selected, and site visits and
assessments were conducted for each location. In addition, two (2) public
outreach meetings scheduled. Site parameters included, but were not limited to
existing facilities and constraints, town location, parking availability, proximity
to abutters, surface and subsurface considerations as well as overall cost. Two
sites, both on Town Properties within connection to the Hingham Recreation
Department - Carlson Complex, were selected. The proposed project site was
selected for several reasons: the connection to the existing Carlson Complex;
ADA general access; remote location from abutters (more than 780 feet) with a
wooded buffer; and the opportunity to redevelop an existing dilapidated
warehouse site.

February 3, 2026
Hingham Conservation Commission
c/o Shannon Palmer, Conservation Officer
Town of Hingham
210 Central Street
Hingham, MA 02043
Re:

Peer Review of Request for Determination of Applicability
Hingham Center for Active Learning, 0 Fort Hill Street, Hingham, MA

Dear Ms. Palmer and members of the Hingham Conservation Commission:
The Horsley Witten Group, Inc. (HW) is pleased to provide this review of the Request for
Determination of Applicability (RDA) and supporting materials submitted by SLR International
Corporation (SLR) on behalf of the Applicant, EDM Studio, Inc., for the above referenced Site
off Bare Cove Park Drive in Hingham, MA. The Hingham Conservation Commission (the
“Commission”) is seeking to have HW confirm whether the wetland resource areas at this Site
are accurately delineated in accordance with the Massachusetts Wetlands Protection Act
(M.G.L. Ch. 131 § 40) and its implementing Regulations (310 CMR 10.00) (the “WPA”) as well
as under the Town of Hingham Wetlands Protection Bylaw, General Bylaws of the Town of
Hingham, Article 22, and associated Hingham Wetland Regulations (the “local regulations”).
HW reviewed the Applicant’s RDA submission for confirmation of vegetated wetlands within an
approximately 13.8-acre portion of the 462.6-acre parcel (Assessor’s Map 69, Parcel 44) (the
“Site”). A Potential Vernal Pool (PVP #10722) exists within one of the two areas delineated as
vegetated wetland at the Site; its boundary was not originally delineated by SLR. An unnamed
perennial stream is present within the other area of vegetated wetland at the Site, identified as
“Perennial Watercourse (MassDEP)” on the existing conditions plan. The stream was not
included in HW’s on-site review as we understand that its Mean Annual High Water lines
(MAHW)/Banks were previously confirmed under a separate an Order of Resource Area
Determination (ORAD) issued by the Commission (DEP File No. 034-1509).
The scope of this review is limited to the portions of wetland boundaries within the Site, located
north of Bare Cove Park Drive, west of undeveloped forested area on the adjacent parcels, and
east of additional undeveloped forested area within the referenced parcel. Two buildings and
one associated access drive is located within the Site.

Materials Reviewed
HW has received the following materials for this review:
• Request for Determination of Applicability signed and dated November 19, 2025 (3 pages);

by SLR International Corporation, dated November 19, 2025, including DEP Bordering

• Hingham Center for Active Learning1, Wetland Delineation Comparison, Bare Cove Park
