# State Housing Oversight, Chapter 40B Filings & EOHLC/MassHousing Regulatory Review: 100 Beal Street (Hingham, MA)

<!-- File Version: state_housing_and_40B_filings_v1.md -->

**Site:** 100 Beal Street, Hingham, MA 02043 (School Tract II, Map 58, Lot 23)  
**State Regulatory Bodies:** 
- Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities (EOHLC, formerly DHCD)
- MassHousing (Massachusetts Housing Finance Agency)
- Massachusetts Housing Partnership (MHP)
- Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection (MassDEP)
**Statutory Authorities:** M.G.L. c. 121B, § 34; M.G.L. c. 40B, §§ 20–23; 760 CMR 56.00 (Comprehensive Permit Regulations); M.G.L. c. 30B, § 16.

---

## 1. Overview & Regulatory Jurisdiction

The planned development of **68 units of affordable senior rental housing** at **100 Beal Street** is governed by an intricate intersection of state public housing statutes, disposition controls under M.G.L. c. 121B, and the Chapter 40B Comprehensive Permit regulatory process.

Because 100 Beal Street was acquired and developed under state-aided housing programs (specifically designated as Department of Mental Health / Department of Social Services special needs public housing, Chapter 689 Program, Project 689-01), the fee title of the property is subject to perpetual commonwealth disposition restrictions.

---

## 2. EOHLC / DHCD Title Encumbrance: M.G.L. c. 121B, § 34

### 2.1 The Statutory Restriction
Under Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 121B, Section 34, no municipal housing authority may sell, lease, transfer, or encumber any portion of real property acquired with commonwealth assistance without:
1. Express written authorization and determination of surplus status by the Secretary of EOHLC;
2. Formal review ensuring that the proposed disposition advances the Commonwealth's public housing and affordable housing priorities;
3. Execution of binding land disposition agreements (LDDA) maintaining long-term affordability restrictions.

### 2.2 Recorded Title Encumbrance
Following disputes between the Town of Hingham and the HHA in 2019 regarding an attempted transfer of 19 acres back to municipal control, DHCD intervened and recorded:
- **Instrument:** *Notice of Statutory Transfer Restriction*
- **Registry:** Plymouth County Registry of Deeds, **Book 51379, Page 244** (Recorded July 18, 2019).
- **Substantive Finding:** EOHLC formally confirmed that the HHA cannot alienate School Tract II without state sign-off, effectively reserving the 8.6-acre developable portion for subsidized housing development.

---

## 3. Chapter 40B Permitting Framework & Project Eligibility (PEL)

### 3.1 Necessity of Chapter 40B
The 100 Beal Street parcel is situated within an **Official and Open Space District (OO)** under the Town of Hingham Zoning By-Law. Multi-family residential structures are prohibited by right and cannot be permitted through municipal special permits. Consequently, the HHA and its selected private development partner, **Peabody Properties**, are advancing the 68-unit development via a **Comprehensive Permit pursuant to M.G.L. c. 40B**.

### 3.2 Project Eligibility Letter (PEL) / Site Approval Requirements
To submit a formal Comprehensive Permit application to the Hingham Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA), Peabody Properties and the HHA must obtain a **Project Eligibility Letter (PEL)** (Site Approval) from an authorized Subsidizing Agency:
- **Eligible Subsidizing Agencies:** MassHousing, EOHLC (under the Local Initiative Program / LIP), or the Massachusetts Housing Partnership (MHP).
- **Prerequisites for PEL Issuance (760 CMR 56.04):**
  1. **Site Control:** Demonstrated through the HHA's fee ownership and the executed Land Disposition and Development Agreement (LDDA) / long-term ground lease with Peabody Properties.
  2. **Applicant Eligibility:** Limited dividend entity qualification or non-profit/public housing authority status.
  3. **Preliminary Financial Feasibility:** Demonstration of fundability through state or federal subsidy sources, including Low-Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTC), EOHLC capital subsidies, or MassHousing financing.
  4. **Initial Environmental & Site Review:** Municipal notification and a 30-day municipal comment period, during which the Select Board, Planning Board, and Conservation Commission submit technical concerns to the Subsidizing Agency.

### 3.3 Comparative Beal Street 40B Precedents
Beal Street has been the epicenter of extensive Chapter 40B permitting in Hingham:
- **Broadstone Bare Cove (230 Beal Street / "The Cove"):**
  - Project Eligibility Letter issued by MassHousing on **August 12, 2016** (MassHousing ID: 885).
  - Permitted for 220 units across 5 residential buildings.
  - Constructed adjacent to Bare Cove Park and the MBTA West Hingham commuter rail station.
- **River Stone (Ward Street / French Street):**
  - 36-unit 40B comprehensive permit contested aggressively by the Town of Hingham through the Housing Appeals Committee (HAC), Land Court, and Massachusetts Appeals Court, concluding in final settlement and project completion in November 2025.
- **100 Beal Street (68 Senior Units):**
  - Represents the **fifth major 40B proposal** along the Beal Street corridor.
  - Unlike private commercial 40Bs, 100 Beal Street is sponsored by the municipal housing authority (HHA), creating a distinct regulatory dynamic between the HHA (proponent) and the Town ZBA/Planning Board (reviewing authorities).

---

## 4. Safe Harbor Analysis: Hingham's Statutory Standing under 760 CMR 56.03

### 4.1 Surpassing the 10% Statutory Minimum
Under M.G.L. c. 40B, § 20 and 760 CMR 56.03, municipalities that have exceeded 10% of their total year-round housing units on the state **Subsidized Housing Inventory (SHI)** achieve "Safe Harbor" status:
- Hingham has documented an SHI ratio exceeding 10%, primarily through the addition of large rental developments such as Broadstone Bare Cove and Avalon at Hingham Shipyard.
- **Legal Ramifications:** When a municipality is in Safe Harbor, the local Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA) has the legal authority to **deny** a Chapter 40B Comprehensive Permit or impose conditions without risk of automatic reversal by the state Housing Appeals Committee (HAC), provided the ZBA asserts safe harbor within 15 days of opening the public hearing.

### 4.2 Application to 100 Beal Street
- Because 100 Beal Street is sponsored by the HHA and targets seniors earning at or below 30%, 50%, and 60% of AMI, the project is structured as a collaborative municipal-state development.
- However, as community abutters (such as Craftsman Village) have asserted, the Town's Safe Harbor status grants the ZBA legal standing to enforce strict compliance with local wetland bylaws and require scale reductions (e.g., from 68 units down to 46 units) if local environmental impacts on Tucker's Swamp and the Back River ACEC are determined to outweigh local housing needs.

---

## 5. Summary Table: Key State Administrative Records

| Agency | Record / Instrument | Date | Relevance to 100 Beal Street |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **DHCD / EOHLC** | Legal Warning Letter | April 19, 2019 | Barred unilateral conveyance of School Tract II to Town under c. 121B, § 34. |
| **DHCD / EOHLC** | Notice of Statutory Transfer Restriction | July 18, 2019 | Recorded encumbrance at Book 51379, Page 244 binding 100 Beal to state housing use. |
| **MassDEP** | ORAD (File No. 034-1509) | Nov 7, 2024 | Three-year validation of BVW, IVW, vernal pool, and ACEC tributary boundaries. |
| **HHA / EOHLC** | Surplus Disposition Authorization | Sept 10, 2024 | Voted 8.6 acres surplus under c. 30B, § 16 for senior housing procurement. |
| **MassHousing / EOHLC** | Chapter 40B PEL Application Scope | 2025–2026 | Application framework for 68 senior rental units (LDDA with Peabody Properties). |


---


## Document: town_documents_and_legal_records_v1.md
- **Relative Path:** `documents/town_documents_and_legal_records_v1.md`

# Municipal Town Records, Legal Agreements, Deed Restrictions, and Environmental Review: 100 Beal Street Senior Affordable Housing (Hingham, MA)

**Document Identifier:** `town_documents_and_legal_records_v1.md`  
**Site:** 100 Beal Street, Hingham, Massachusetts  
**Assessor Parcel ID:** Map 58, Block 0, Lot 23  
**Historical Designation:** School Tract II (Plan Book 17, Page 508)  
**Fee Owner:** Hingham Housing Authority (HHA)  
**Developer Partner:** Peabody Properties  
**Lead Site Planner & Civil Engineer:** Weston & Sampson  
**Key Regulatory Frameworks:** M.G.L. c. 121B, § 34; M.G.L. c. 30B; M.G.L. c. 40B; M.G.L. c. 131, § 40 (Wetlands Protection Act); 310 CMR 10.00; Weymouth Back River Area of Critical Environmental Concern (ACEC); Town of Hingham Wetland Protection By-law (Town Code, Part II, Art. 25).

---

## Executive Overview

The property at **100 Beal Street** is an 8.6-acre developable portion of an overall 15.014-acre parcel owned by the **Hingham Housing Authority (HHA)**. Formally known across historical land records as **"School Tract II"**, the parcel is situated directly adjacent to **Bare Cove Park** and borders the hydrologic watershed of the **Weymouth Back River Area of Critical Environmental Concern (ACEC)**.

The parcel is currently subject to high-profile planning and community deliberation concerning the construction of a **68-unit affordable senior rental housing development** (restricted to seniors aged 62 and older), advanced by the HHA in partnership with selected private developer **Peabody Properties** and engineering/landscape architecture firm **Weston & Sampson**.

This investigative report consolidates the foundational chain of title, municipal agreements, Town Meeting actions, inter-governmental disputes between the Town of Hingham and the HHA/DHCD, state statutory restrictions, procurement records under M.G.L. c. 30B, Chapter 40B comprehensive permitting dynamics, and conservation/environmental adjudications under MassDEP File No. **034-1509**.

---

## 1. Site Identity, Ownership & Land Registry History

### 1.1 Parcel Identification
- **Address:** 100 Beal Street, Hingham, MA 02043
- **Assessor Record:** Map 58, Block 0, Lot 23 (approx. 15.014 total acres; current senior housing disposition area comprises approx. 8.6 acres).
- **Zoning Classification:** **Official and Open Space District (OO)**. Under the Town of Hingham Zoning By-Law, multi-family residential structures are prohibited by right and not permitted via special permit, necessitating a **Comprehensive Permit pursuant to M.G.L. c. 40B**.
- **Historical Military Context:** Formerly part of the federal U.S. Naval Ammunition Depot Hingham (operating from 1903 through the mid-20th century before surplus land was ceded to the Town and commonwealth entities, including Bare Cove Park).

### 1.2 Foundational Subdivision & Deeds (Plymouth County Registry of Deeds)
1. **1972 Subdivision Plan:**
   - **Plan Title:** *"Plan of Land: Beal, West, & Fort Streets, prepared for the Town of Hingham"*
   - **Date / Surveyor:** July 1972, Perkins Engineering, Inc.
   - **Recording:** Plymouth County Registry of Deeds, **Plan Book 17, Page 508** (specifically Sheets 3 and 4).
   - **Tract Definition:** Establishes and delineates **"School Tract II"** (15.014 acres) alongside adjacent municipal tracts including "School Tract IV".

2. **1989 Conveyance to Hingham Housing Authority:**
   - **Grantor:** Inhabitants of the Town of Hingham
   - **Grantee:** Hingham Housing Authority
   - **Date:** March 7, 1989
   - **Recording:** Plymouth County Registry of Deeds, **Book 9097, Page 158**.
   - **Associated Plan:** *"Division of School Tract II, Beal Street, Hingham MA"*, recorded at **Book 9097, Page 160**.
   - **Original Deed Restriction:** The deed contained an explicit restrictive covenant stipulating that the property was to be utilized exclusively as a *"residential educational facility for emotionally disturbed adolescents"* operated by the South Shore Educational Collaborative (SSEC) or an equivalent service entity under state welfare/development contracts.
   - **Existing Built Improvements:** Built in 1989/1990 under state-aided public housing assistance (6 units of special needs residential group housing, historically known as the Beal Street Residential Program / Bay State Community Services facility).

---

## 2. The 2001 Memorandum of Understanding & The Town/HHA Legal Impasse

### 2.1 The 2001 Memorandum of Agreement
On **June 12, 2001**, the Town of Hingham and the HHA executed a **Memorandum of Agreement (MOU)** concerning School Tract II / 100 Beal Street, followed by formal correspondence dated **July 31, 2001**. 

- **Substance of the MOU:** The Town had funded and performed significant municipal infrastructure work and site remediation/demolition on School Tract II utilizing local taxpayer capital.
- **The Reciprocal Obligation:** In exchange for the Town's capital expenditures on site improvements, the MOU contemplated that excess, undeveloped portions of School Tract II (approximately 8 to 19 acres outside the immediate footprint of the special needs residential building) would eventually be deeded or transferred back to the Town of Hingham for municipal/conservation/open space utilization.

### 2.2 Impasse, Executive Session, and Litigation Vote (2019)
Over the following 18 years, the contemplated land transfer was never consummated. By early 2019, relations between the Hingham Board of Selectmen (now Select Board) and the HHA deteriorated into a formal legal impasse:

- **Board of Selectmen Executive Session — February 26, 2019:**
  - Convened at 6:45 PM under Purpose 3 of the Open Meeting Law (litigation strategy).
  - Town Real Estate Counsel **Susan Murphy** provided a full brief on the 2001 MOU and the failure of HHA to convey the property.
  - Selectman **Karen Johnson** placed on record that Town taxpayers had directly funded extensive site and demolition work at 100 Beal Street with the explicit legal expectation of property transfer.
  - **Vote:** The Board of Selectmen voted unanimously (3–0) to **file litigation against the Hingham Housing Authority** to compel legal enforcement and specific performance of the 2001 agreement.

### 2.3 The Attempted 2019 Conveyance and DHCD Intervention
Following pressure from the Town's litigation posture:
- **June 5, 2019 Special Meeting of HHA:** The HHA Board of Commissioners voted to approve the transfer of the 19-acre parcel (School Tract II) back to the Town of Hingham.
- **State Intervention (DHCD / M.G.L. c. 121B, § 34):**
  - Upon learning of the pending transfer, the **Massachusetts Department of Housing and Community Development (DHCD)**, now the **Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities (EOHLC)**, intervened immediately.
  - DHCD legal counsel issued formal warning letters on **April 19, 2019**, and **July 19, 2019**, declaring the proposed transfer illegal under state housing law.
  - **Statutory Mandate:** Under **M.G.L. c. 121B, § 34**, any parcel acquired or developed with state financial assistance or held under a Contract for Financial Assistance (CFA) is subject to strict state oversight. A local housing authority has no legal power to dispose of, convey, or encumber public housing land without express prior written approval from DHCD/EOHLC and review by the Massachusetts Office of the Attorney General.
  - **Clouding Title / Statutory Notice:** To prevent any unauthorized transfer at the local level, DHCD executed and recorded an encumbrance directly onto the property title:
    - **Instrument:** *Notice of Statutory Transfer Restriction*
    - **Recording Date:** July 18, 2019
    - **Recording Registry:** Plymouth County Registry of Deeds, **Book 51379, Page 244**.
    - **Legal Effect:** Creates a perpetual, blanket statutory title restriction confirming that no conveyance or transfer of School Tract II / 100 Beal Street can occur without formal EOHLC written authorization, effectively blocking the Town's attempt to seize or claim the land.

### 2.4 Formal Rescission by HHA (September 7, 2021)
At the HHA Board of Commissioners meeting on **September 7, 2021**, acting on joint advice from DHCD legal counsel and municipal counsel, the Board formally voted **4–0 to RESCIND** the June 5, 2019 motion that had authorized the transfer to the Town. This solidified the HHA's sole legal ownership and retention of School Tract II for public/affordable housing development.

---

## 3. Chapter 30B Procurement & Developer RFP

Having reasserted exclusive control over School Tract II, the Hingham Housing Authority initiated steps to activate the surplus land for new affordable housing production.

### 3.1 Board Authorization & Surplus Declaration (September 10, 2024)
At its regular meeting on **September 10, 2024**, the HHA Board of Commissioners voted to:
1. Formally declare approximately 8.6 acres of the 100 Beal Street property as "excess / surplus property" pursuant to public housing modernization and disposition guidelines.
2. Solicit competitive development proposals under the **Massachusetts Uniform Procurement Act (M.G.L. c. 30B, § 16)** governing real property disposition exceeding $35,000 in assessed value.
3. Authorize Executive Director Randy Waters to prepare and issue a competitive **Request for Proposals (RFP)**.

### 3.2 The Request for Proposals (RFP) Specifications
- **RFP Title:** *Request for Proposals for the Development of Affordable Senior Rental Housing at 100 Beal Street, Hingham, MA*
- **Issuance Date:** April 2025
- **Pre-Proposal Meeting & Site Tour:** May 1, 2025
- **Proposal Submission Deadline:** **June 11, 2025, at 4:00 PM EST**
- **Submission Requirements:** 1 original in a 3-ring binder, 5 hard copies, and 1 complete digital file on USB; electronic/fax submissions rejected.
- **Contract Mechanism:** The HHA structured the transaction not as an outright fee simple sale, but as a long-term ground lease under a **Land Disposition and Development Agreement (LDDA)**, ensuring that the fee title remains anchored with the Housing Authority while private development partners finance, construct, operate, and manage the facility.
- **Target Demographics & Units:** 
  - Originally scoped at approximately **60 units** of deeply affordable and mixed-income senior rental apartments (age 62+).
  - Income tiers targeting households earning at or below 30%, 50%, and 60% of Area Median Income (AMI).
- **Award:** Following evaluation by the HHA Selection Committee, the contract was officially awarded to **Peabody Properties**, with site civil engineering and landscape architecture spearheaded by **Weston & Sampson**.

---

## 4. Chapter 40B Comprehensive Permitting & State Subsidizing Filings

### 4.1 Permitting Route Under M.G.L. c. 40B
Because the property is zoned **Official and Open Space (OO)**, multi-family residential housing is barred by local zoning. Consequently, the HHA and Peabody Properties have chosen to permit the development via a **Comprehensive Permit (Chapter 40B)** before the **Hingham Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA)**:
- Chapter 40B enables the developer to request waivers from local bylaws—including density, dimensional requirements, building height, parking ratios, and local wetland bylaws—provided the project meets health, safety, and environmental standards.
- Under state guidelines, the HHA and Peabody Properties prepared an application for a **Project Eligibility Letter (PEL)** from the subsidizing agency (such as **MassHousing**, **EOHLC**, or the **Massachusetts Housing Partnership / MHP**).

### 4.2 Expansion to 68 Units & Community Pushback (2026)
Between late 2025 and mid-2026, Peabody Properties refined the architectural and site civil designs with Weston & Sampson, expanding the planned development from the RFP baseline of 60 units to **68 units**:
- **Structure:** A proposed 3-story residential structure designed to minimize footprint impact by nestling into existing woodland topography.
- **Local Controversy:** 
  - In August 2026, community debate intensified over the scale of the 68-unit proposal.
  - A prominent opinion editorial published in the *Hingham Anchor* on August 18, 2026 (authored by resident Shannon Brinkley) questioned the expansion from early historical concepts (20–48 units) to 68 units on land zoned Official and Open Space.
  - Concerns were raised regarding the potential use of 40B waivers to override local wetland protection buffer standards, especially given that Hingham has already surpassed the statutory 10% Subsidized Housing Inventory (SHI) threshold (the safe harbor benchmark under 760 CMR 56.03). Under safe harbor, the ZBA possesses greater statutory latitude to deny or condition 40B applications unless the subsidizing agency or housing authority reaches an accord with the municipality.

---

## 5. Environmental Adjudications & Physical Site Constraints

The 100 Beal Street parcel is one of the most environmentally sensitive development sites in Hingham due to three intersecting ecological boundaries:
1. **Weymouth Back River Area of Critical Environmental Concern (ACEC):** Portions of the southern and eastern sectors of the parcel drain into tributaries and wetland systems designated as **Outstanding Resource Waters (ORW)** tributary to the Back River ACEC.
2. **Bare Cove Park & Wildlife Refuge:** Directly borders the northern and western margins of Bare Cove Park, an environmentally protected municipal sanctuary home to sensitive bird nesting habitats and vernal pools.
3. **Internal Wetland Systems & Hydrology:** A substantial portion of the parcel consists of poorly drained soils, high groundwater tables, and forested wetlands.

```
                  +----------------------------------------------+
                  |               BEAL STREET                     |
                  +----------------------------------------------+
                                         |
                                         v
       +------------------------------------------------------------------+
       | MAP 58, LOT 23 ("SCHOOL TRACT II" - TOTAL 15.014 ACRES)           |
       |                                                                  |
       |   +--------------------------+                                   |
       |   | Existing 1-Story Group   |   Undeveloped Developable Area    |
       |   | Home Facility (Built '89)|   (~8.6 Acres) - Peabody/W&S      |
       |   +--------------------------+   Proposed 3-Story / 68 Units     |
       |                                                                  |
       |   ------------------ WETLAND BOUNDARIES ----------------------   |
       |   - BVW 1, 2, 3 (Bordering Vegetative Wetlands)                  |
       |   - IVW 1, 2 (Isolated Vegetative Wetlands)                      |
       |   - Certified / Delineated Vernal Pool (DEP # 034-1509)          |
       +------------------------------------------------------------------+
             |                                              |
             v                                              v
  +----------------------+                      +------------------------+
  |    BARE COVE PARK    |                      | WEYMOUTH BACK RIVER    |
  |   WILDLIFE REFUGE    |                      |      A.C.E.C.          |
  +----------------------+                      +------------------------+
```

### 5.1 Conservation Commission ANRAD / ORAD Review (MassDEP No. 034-1509)
To legally fix and confirm wetland resource boundaries prior to filing formal Chapter 40B site designs, the applicant team retained **Lucas Environmental, LLC** (represented by environmental scientist Christopher Lucas) and **Control Point Associates, Inc.** to conduct exhaustive site delineations:

1. **ANRAD Filing:**
   - **MassDEP File Number:** **034-1509**
   - **Applicant Representative:** Christopher Lucas, Lucas Environmental, LLC
   - **Civil Delineation Plan:** Prepared by Control Point Associates, Inc., dated September 9, 2024.
   - **Resource Areas Identified:**
     - Three separate systems of **Bordering Vegetative Wetlands (BVW)** subject to jurisdiction under M.G.L. c. 131, § 40 and 310 CMR 10.55.
     - Two systems of **Isolated Vegetative Wetlands (IVW)** protected under the Town of Hingham Wetlands Protection By-Law.
     - A verified **Vernal Pool** located in the southwestern quadrant of the parcel, triggering critical 100-foot no-disturbance and buffer zone protections under local bylaws.
     - 200-foot **Riverfront Area** and Mean Annual High Water (MAHW) lines associated with ACEC-tributary streams.

2. **Order of Resource Area Delineation (ORAD):**
   - **Public Hearing:** Opened and concluded on **November 4, 2024**, before the Hingham Conservation Commission.
   - **Vote:** The Conservation Commission voted **5–0** to approve and issue a comprehensive Order of Resource Area Delineation (issued on **November 7, 2024**).
   - **Significance:** The ORAD validates all boundary flags on the Control Point Associates plan for three years, binding any future Notice of Intent (NOI) or Chapter 40B site plan review to these exact wetland boundaries.

---

## 6. Synthesis of Key Legal & Municipal Records

| Date | Entity / Agency | Record / Instrument | Citation / Reference | Substantive Outcome / Legal Significance |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **July 1972** | Town of Hingham / Perkins Engineering | Subdivision Plan: Beal, West & Fort Streets | Plan Book 17, Page 508 | Established boundaries of School Tract II (15.014 acres). |
| **March 7, 1989** | Town of Hingham to HHA | Property Deed & Plan | Book 9097, Page 158; Plan Book 9097, Page 160 | Conveyed School Tract II to HHA; restricted use to adolescent educational facility. |
| **June 12, 2001** | Town of Hingham & HHA | Memorandum of Agreement (MOU) | HHA Minutes / Selectmen Records | Contemplated return of excess land to Town in exchange for municipal infrastructure/demolition costs. |

---

## 7. Conclusions and Key Strategic Insights

1. **Clear Fee Ownership with State Protection:** 
   Although the Town of Hingham attempted to claim School Tract II based on the 2001 MOU and taxpayer-funded demolition work, the intervention of DHCD/EOHLC and the recording of the **Notice of Statutory Transfer Restriction at Book 51379, Page 244** confirms that fee title remains legally unassailable with the Hingham Housing Authority. The Town cannot compel a unilateral transfer of this property.

2. **Zoning Barrier and Chapter 40B Necessity:** 
   Because the parcel is zoned Official and Open Space (OO), the development cannot proceed through standard municipal special permits or site plan review. Chapter 40B is legally mandatory to bypass the OO zoning prohibition.

3. **Safe Harbor Vulnerability:** 
   Because Hingham currently meets the 10% Subsidized Housing Inventory (SHI) threshold, the Hingham Zoning Board of Appeals is not statutorily compelled to grant wholesale zoning waivers if it determines that local health, environmental, or open space concerns outweigh the regional need for affordable housing. This heightens the importance of community negotiations between Peabody Properties, the HHA, and the Town.

4. **Rigid Wetland and ACEC Envelope:** 
   With MassDEP File No. **034-1509** fully adjudicated and the ORAD issued on November 7, 2024, the developable footprint of the 8.6-acre parcel is strictly constrained by confirmed Bordering Vegetative Wetlands, Isolated Vegetative Wetlands, a vernal pool, and the adjacent Weymouth Back River ACEC. The three-story, 68-unit site plan engineered by Weston & Sampson must navigate these setbacks or seek specific bylaw waivers through the 40B comprehensive permit.

# Municipal Town Records, Legal Agreements, Deed Restrictions, and Environmental Review: 100 Beal Street Senior Affordable Housing (Hingham, MA)

**Document Identifier:** `town_documents_and_legal_records_v2.md`  
**Site:** 100 Beal Street, Hingham, Massachusetts  
**Assessor Parcel ID:** Map 58, Block 0, Lot 23  
**Historical Designation:** School Tract II (Plan Book 17, Page 508)  
**Fee Owner:** Hingham Housing Authority (HHA)  
**Developer Partner:** Peabody Properties  
**Lead Site Planner & Civil Engineer:** Weston & Sampson  
**Key Regulatory Frameworks:** M.G.L. c. 121B, § 34; M.G.L. c. 30B; M.G.L. c. 40B; M.G.L. c. 131, § 40 (Wetlands Protection Act); 310 CMR 10.00; Weymouth Back River Area of Critical Environmental Concern (ACEC); Town of Hingham Wetland Protection By-law (Town Code, Part II, Art. 25).

---

## Executive Overview

The property at **100 Beal Street** is an 8.6-acre developable portion of an overall 15.014-acre parcel owned by the **Hingham Housing Authority (HHA)**. Formally known across historical land records as **"School Tract II"**, the parcel is situated directly adjacent to **Bare Cove Park** and borders the hydrologic watershed of the **Weymouth Back River Area of Critical Environmental Concern (ACEC)**.

The parcel is currently subject to high-profile planning and community deliberation concerning the construction of a **68-unit affordable senior rental housing development** (restricted to seniors aged 62 and older), advanced by the HHA in partnership with selected private developer **Peabody Properties** and engineering/landscape architecture firm **Weston & Sampson**.

This investigative report consolidates the foundational chain of title, municipal agreements, Town Meeting actions, inter-governmental disputes between the Town of Hingham and the HHA/DHCD, state statutory restrictions, procurement records under M.G.L. c. 30B, Chapter 40B comprehensive permitting dynamics, and conservation/environmental adjudications under MassDEP File No. **034-1509**.

---

## 1. Site Identity, Ownership & Land Registry History

### 1.1 Parcel Identification
- **Address:** 100 Beal Street, Hingham, MA 02043
- **Assessor Record:** Map 58, Block 0, Lot 23 (approx. 15.014 total acres; current senior housing disposition area comprises approx. 8.6 acres).
- **Zoning Classification:** **Official and Open Space District (OO)**. Under the Town of Hingham Zoning By-Law, multi-family residential structures are prohibited by right and not permitted via special permit, necessitating a **Comprehensive Permit pursuant to M.G.L. c. 40B**.
- **Historical Military Context:** Formerly part of the federal U.S. Naval Ammunition Depot Hingham (operating from 1903 through the mid-20th century before surplus land was ceded to the Town and commonwealth entities, including Bare Cove Park).

### 1.2 Foundational Subdivision & Deeds (Plymouth County Registry of Deeds)
1. **1972 Subdivision Plan:**
   - **Plan Title:** *"Plan of Land: Beal, West, & Fort Streets, prepared for the Town of Hingham"*
   - **Date / Surveyor:** July 1972, Perkins Engineering, Inc.
   - **Recording:** Plymouth County Registry of Deeds, **Plan Book 17, Page 508** (specifically Sheets 3 and 4).
   - **Tract Definition:** Establishes and delineates **"School Tract II"** (15.014 acres) alongside adjacent municipal tracts including "School Tract IV".

2. **1989 Conveyance to Hingham Housing Authority:**
   - **Grantor:** Inhabitants of the Town of Hingham
   - **Grantee:** Hingham Housing Authority
   - **Date:** March 7, 1989
   - **Recording:** Plymouth County Registry of Deeds, **Book 9097, Page 158**.
   - **Associated Plan:** *"Division of School Tract II, Beal Street, Hingham MA"*, recorded at **Book 9097, Page 160**.
   - **Original Deed Restriction:** The deed contained an explicit restrictive covenant stipulating that the property was to be utilized exclusively as a *"residential educational facility for emotionally disturbed adolescents"* operated by the South Shore Educational Collaborative (SSEC) or an equivalent service entity under state welfare/development contracts.
   - **Existing Built Improvements:** Built in 1989/1990 under state-aided public housing assistance (6 units of special needs residential group housing, historically known as the Beal Street Residential Program / Bay State Community Services facility).

---

## 2. The 2001 Memorandum of Understanding & The Town/HHA Legal Impasse

### 2.1 The 2001 Memorandum of Agreement
On **June 12, 2001**, the Town of Hingham and the HHA executed a **Memorandum of Agreement (MOU)** concerning School Tract II / 100 Beal Street, followed by formal correspondence dated **July 31, 2001**. 

- **Substance of the MOU:** The Town had funded and performed significant municipal infrastructure work and site remediation/demolition on School Tract II utilizing local taxpayer capital.
- **The Reciprocal Obligation:** In exchange for the Town's capital expenditures on site improvements, the MOU contemplated that excess, undeveloped portions of School Tract II (approximately 8 to 19 acres outside the immediate footprint of the special needs residential building) would eventually be deeded or transferred back to the Town of Hingham for municipal/conservation/open space utilization.

### 2.2 Impasse, Executive Session, and Litigation Vote (2019)
Over the following 18 years, the contemplated land transfer was never consummated. By early 2019, relations between the Hingham Board of Selectmen (now Select Board) and the HHA deteriorated into a formal legal impasse:

- **Board of Selectmen Executive Session — February 26, 2019:**
  - Convened at 6:45 PM under Purpose 3 of the Open Meeting Law (litigation strategy).
  - Town Real Estate Counsel **Susan Murphy** provided a full brief on the 2001 MOU and the failure of HHA to convey the property.
  - Selectman **Karen Johnson** placed on record that Town taxpayers had directly funded extensive site and demolition work at 100 Beal Street with the explicit legal expectation of property transfer.
  - **Vote:** The Board of Selectmen voted unanimously (3–0) to **file litigation against the Hingham Housing Authority** to compel legal enforcement and specific performance of the 2001 agreement.

### 2.3 The Attempted 2019 Conveyance and DHCD Intervention
Following pressure from the Town's litigation posture:
- **June 5, 2019 Special Meeting of HHA:** The HHA Board of Commissioners voted to approve the transfer of the 19-acre parcel (School Tract II) back to the Town of Hingham.
- **State Intervention (DHCD / M.G.L. c. 121B, § 34):**
  - Upon learning of the pending transfer, the **Massachusetts Department of Housing and Community Development (DHCD)**, now the **Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities (EOHLC)**, intervened immediately.
  - DHCD legal counsel issued formal warning letters on **April 19, 2019**, and **July 19, 2019**, declaring the proposed transfer illegal under state housing law.
  - **Statutory Mandate:** Under **M.G.L. c. 121B, § 34**, any parcel acquired or developed with state financial assistance or held under a Contract for Financial Assistance (CFA) is subject to strict state oversight. A local housing authority has no legal power to dispose of, convey, or encumber public housing land without express prior written approval from DHCD/EOHLC and review by the Massachusetts Office of the Attorney General.
  - **Clouding Title / Statutory Notice:** To prevent any unauthorized transfer at the local level, DHCD executed and recorded an encumbrance directly onto the property title:
    - **Instrument:** *Notice of Statutory Transfer Restriction*
    - **Recording Date:** July 18, 2019
    - **Recording Registry:** Plymouth County Registry of Deeds, **Book 51379, Page 244**.
    - **Legal Effect:** Creates a perpetual, blanket statutory title restriction confirming that no conveyance or transfer of School Tract II / 100 Beal Street can occur without formal EOHLC written authorization, effectively blocking the Town's attempt to seize or claim the land.

### 2.4 Formal Rescission by HHA (September 7, 2021)
At the HHA Board of Commissioners meeting on **September 7, 2021**, acting on joint advice from DHCD legal counsel and municipal counsel, the Board formally voted **4–0 to RESCIND** the June 5, 2019 motion that had authorized the transfer to the Town. This solidified the HHA's sole legal ownership and retention of School Tract II for public/affordable housing development.

---

## 3. Chapter 30B Procurement & Developer RFP

Having reasserted exclusive control over School Tract II, the Hingham Housing Authority initiated steps to activate the surplus land for new affordable housing production.

### 3.1 Board Authorization & Surplus Declaration (September 10, 2024)
At its regular meeting on **September 10, 2024**, the HHA Board of Commissioners voted to:
1. Formally declare approximately 8.6 acres of the 100 Beal Street property as "excess / surplus property" pursuant to public housing modernization and disposition guidelines.
2. Solicit competitive development proposals under the **Massachusetts Uniform Procurement Act (M.G.L. c. 30B, § 16)** governing real property disposition exceeding $35,000 in assessed value.
3. Authorize Executive Director Randy Waters to prepare and issue a competitive **Request for Proposals (RFP)**.

### 3.2 The Request for Proposals (RFP) Specifications
- **RFP Title:** *Request for Proposals for the Development of Affordable Senior Rental Housing at 100 Beal Street, Hingham, MA*
- **Issuance Date:** April 2025
- **Pre-Proposal Meeting & Site Tour:** May 1, 2025
- **Proposal Submission Deadline:** **June 11, 2025, at 4:00 PM EST**
- **Submission Requirements:** 1 original in a 3-ring binder, 5 hard copies, and 1 complete digital file on USB; electronic/fax submissions rejected.
- **Contract Mechanism:** The HHA structured the transaction not as an outright fee simple sale, but as a long-term ground lease under a **Land Disposition and Development Agreement (LDDA)**, ensuring that the fee title remains anchored with the Housing Authority while private development partners finance, construct, operate, and manage the facility.
- **Target Demographics & Units:** 
  - Originally scoped at approximately **60 units** of deeply affordable and mixed-income senior rental apartments (age 62+).
  - Income tiers targeting households earning at or below 30%, 50%, and 60% of Area Median Income (AMI).
- **Award:** Following evaluation by the HHA Selection Committee, the contract was officially awarded to **Peabody Properties**, with site civil engineering and landscape architecture spearheaded by **Weston & Sampson**.

---

## 4. Chapter 40B Comprehensive Permitting & State Subsidizing Filings

### 4.1 Permitting Route Under M.G.L. c. 40B
Because the property is zoned **Official and Open Space (OO)**, multi-family residential housing is barred by local zoning. Consequently, the HHA and Peabody Properties have chosen to permit the development via a **Comprehensive Permit (Chapter 40B)** before the **Hingham Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA)**:
- Chapter 40B enables the developer to request waivers from local bylaws—including density, dimensional requirements, building height, parking ratios, and local wetland bylaws—provided the project meets health, safety, and environmental standards.
- Under state guidelines, the HHA and Peabody Properties prepared an application for a **Project Eligibility Letter (PEL)** from the subsidizing agency (such as **MassHousing**, **EOHLC**, or the **Massachusetts Housing Partnership / MHP**).

### 4.2 Expansion to 68 Units & Community Pushback (2026)
Between late 2025 and mid-2026, Peabody Properties refined the architectural and site civil designs with Weston & Sampson, expanding the planned development from the RFP baseline of 60 units to **68 units**:
- **Structure:** A proposed 3-story residential structure designed to minimize footprint impact by nestling into existing woodland topography.
- **Local Controversy:** 
  - In August 2026, community debate intensified over the scale of the 68-unit proposal.
  - A prominent opinion editorial published in the *Hingham Anchor* on August 18, 2026 (authored by resident Shannon Brinkley) questioned the expansion from early historical concepts (20–48 units) to 68 units on land zoned Official and Open Space.
  - Concerns were raised regarding the potential use of 40B waivers to override local wetland protection buffer standards, especially given that Hingham has already surpassed the statutory 10% Subsidized Housing Inventory (SHI) threshold (the safe harbor benchmark under 760 CMR 56.03). Under safe harbor, the ZBA possesses greater statutory latitude to deny or condition 40B applications unless the subsidizing agency or housing authority reaches an accord with the municipality.

### 4.3 State Subsidizing Agency & Project Eligibility Letter (PEL) Dynamics
Under 760 CMR 56.04, Peabody Properties and the HHA are required to secure a Project Eligibility Letter (PEL) from an authorized state subsidizing agency prior to opening formal hearings before the Hingham ZBA:
- **Subsidizing Entities:** MassHousing, EOHLC (under the Local Initiative Program / LIP), or the Massachusetts Housing Partnership (MHP).
- **Required Findings:** The subsidizing agency must evaluate preliminary site layouts, environmental sensitivities, municipal comments (issued during the 30-day chief elected official review window), and financial feasibility under state low-income housing tax credit (LIHTC) and subsidy guidelines.
- **Corridor Context:** This filing represents the fifth major 40B application along Beal Street, following the precedent set by *Broadstone Bare Cove* (230 Beal Street, PEL issued by MassHousing on August 12, 2016).

---

## 5. Environmental Adjudications, Physical Site Constraints & Bare Cove Park

The 100 Beal Street parcel is one of the most environmentally sensitive development sites in Hingham due to three intersecting ecological boundaries:
1. **Weymouth Back River Area of Critical Environmental Concern (ACEC):** Portions of the southern and eastern sectors of the parcel drain into tributaries and wetland systems designated as **Outstanding Resource Waters (ORW)** tributary to the Back River ACEC.
2. **Bare Cove Park & Wildlife Refuge:** Directly borders the northern and western margins of Bare Cove Park, an environmentally protected municipal sanctuary home to sensitive bird nesting habitats and vernal pools.
3. **Internal Wetland Systems & Hydrology:** A substantial portion of the parcel consists of poorly drained soils, high groundwater tables, and forested wetlands.

       |                                                                  |

       |   | Home Facility (Built '89)|   (~8.6 Acres) - Peabody/W&S      |

       |                                                                  |
       |   ------------------ WETLAND BOUNDARIES ----------------------   |

### 5.1 Conservation Commission ANRAD / ORAD Review (MassDEP No. 034-1509)
To legally fix and confirm wetland resource boundaries prior to filing formal Chapter 40B site designs, the applicant team retained **Lucas Environmental, LLC** (represented by environmental scientist Christopher Lucas) and **Control Point Associates, Inc.** to conduct exhaustive site delineations:

1. **ANRAD Filing:**
   - **MassDEP File Number:** **034-1509**
   - **Applicant Representative:** Christopher Lucas, Lucas Environmental, LLC
   - **Civil Delineation Plan:** Prepared by Control Point Associates, Inc., dated September 9, 2024.
   - **Resource Areas Identified:**
     - Three separate systems of **Bordering Vegetative Wetlands (BVW)** subject to jurisdiction under M.G.L. c. 131, § 40 and 310 CMR 10.55.
     - Two systems of **Isolated Vegetative Wetlands (IVW)** protected under the Town of Hingham Wetlands Protection By-Law.
     - A verified **Vernal Pool** located in the southwestern quadrant of the parcel, triggering critical 100-foot no-disturbance and buffer zone protections under local bylaws.
     - 200-foot **Riverfront Area** and Mean Annual High Water (MAHW) lines associated with ACEC-tributary streams.

2. **Order of Resource Area Delineation (ORAD):**
   - **Public Hearing:** Opened and concluded on **November 4, 2024**, before the Hingham Conservation Commission.
   - **Vote:** The Conservation Commission voted **5–0** to approve and issue a comprehensive Order of Resource Area Delineation (issued on **November 7, 2024**).
   - **Significance:** The ORAD validates all boundary flags on the Control Point Associates plan for three years, binding any future Notice of Intent (NOI) or Chapter 40B site plan review to these exact wetland boundaries.

### 5.2 Tucker's Swamp Hydrology & Bare Cove Park Committee Review
- **Hydrological Connection:** The wetlands at 100 Beal Street directly feed **Tucker's Swamp**, which drains via **Hockley Run** to Beal's Cove in the Weymouth Back River.
- **Bare Cove Park Committee (BCPC) & Public Deliberation:** The BCPC and environmental advocates raised concerns regarding cumulative watershed impacts from perimeter development.
- **Town Meeting Determination (April 27, 2026):** Town Meeting voters decisively defeated the proposed municipal Center for Active Living (CAL) inside Bare Cove Park, rejecting deforestation and paving within the park boundary and shifting heightened scrutiny onto the remaining developments along the park periphery—predominantly 100 Beal Street.

## 7. Conclusions and Key Strategic Insights

1. **Clear Fee Ownership with State Protection:** 
   Although the Town of Hingham attempted to claim School Tract II based on the 2001 MOU and taxpayer-funded demolition work, the intervention of DHCD/EOHLC and the recording of the **Notice of Statutory Transfer Restriction at Book 51379, Page 244** confirms that fee title remains legally unassailable with the Hingham Housing Authority. 3. **Safe Harbor Vulnerability:**

This heightens the importance of community negotiations between Peabody Properties, the HHA, and the Town.

4. **Rigid Wetland and ACEC Envelope:**

Note that the Applicant is NOT seeing confirmation of any off-site flagging in the list above; however,
the Applicant is seeking confirmation of the 100-Foot Buffer Zone and RFA that extend into the site from
the off-site resource areas.
The Applicant respectfully requests that the Conservation Commission issue an Order of Resource Area
Delineation under the Wetlands Protection Act and the Town of Hingham Wetlands Protection Bylaw
confirming the accuracy of the characterization and delineation of the areas noted above as described in
this ANRAD application and shown on accompanying ALTA/NSPS Land Title Survey.
Enclosed please find one (1) original and one (1) copy of the ANRAD submittal and Survey Plans. The
ANRAD application package includes the WPA Form 4A, local ANRAD forms, figures, Wetland
Summary Letter and BVW Determination Forms, photographic documentation, abutter notification, and
Survey Plans. A link to an electronic copy of the pdf file of the ANRAD application and supporting
documentation will be provided concurrently with this submittal via email. We respectfully request that
you place this matter on your agenda for the November 4, 2024, Public Hearing.
If you have any questions, please do not hesitate to contact me at 617.405.4140 or cml@lucasenviro.com.

APPENDIX C
Policy on Receipt of Information
(Revised March 4, 2024)

1. New applications/filings must be submitted to the Conservation office (by certified mail or hand delivery)
in accordance with the Commission's Meeting Schedule and Deadlines to facilitate the placement of the
legal advertisement and to allow timely review by the Conservation Officer. Conservation staff will
review the application for administrative completeness. Upon receipt of a complete application, a hearing
or meeting will be scheduled in accordance with the 310 CMR 10.05(5) and the Wetland Regulations,
Section 7.6.
2. If deemed necessary, based on the Commission’s meeting schedule, Conservation staff may request the
applicant voluntarily waive the 21 day statutory deadline for holding a public hearing or issuing a
Determination of Applicability.
3. Requests for additional information may be made by the Commission members or their agent to clarify
the scope of the project or determine compliance with the 310 CMR 10.00 and/or the Hingham Wetland
Regulations. Such requests, if not made at the public hearing, will be communicated to the applicant or
their representative as promptly as possible.
4. Additional information requested by the Commission or their agent in accordance with No.3, must be
submitted to the Conservation office (hard copy and electronic copy) a minimum of 7 days prior to the
meeting date, on Monday by 4PM. If the office is closed on Monday due to a holiday, the information is
due on the preceding Thursday by 4PM. Revisions submitted after the established deadline may not
receive a timely review, thereby resulting in a continuance to the next available meeting.
5. The Commission may engage the peer review services of an outside consultant as provided by M.G.L.
Ch. 44, § 53G, to be paid for by the applicant, for specific expert review deemed necessary to come to a
final decision on a submitted application. Specific consultant services may include but are not limited to,
review of a Notice of Intent, Wetland Resource Area Delineation, Stormwater/Drainage Reports, etc. The
consultant shall be chosen by the Conservation Commission by vote at the public hearing, and report only
to the Commission or its agent. Requested additional information/revisions by the peer reviewer is
required a minimum of two weeks prior to the hearing date.
5. All supplemental documentation and revised plans must include a revision date and must be date stamped
by the Conservation office upon receipt. If this information is not present, the documents may be
considered incomplete and may not receive a timely review, thereby resulting in a continuance to the next
available meeting.
6. Please note that all supplemental documentation and revised plans submitted to the Commission for a
pending application, subject to the MA Wetlands Protection Act, must also be sent to the DEP Southeast
Regional Office, 20 Riverside Dr., Lakeville, MA 02347

The Hingham Conservation Commission is committed to a thorough and timely review of each application and an
efficient hearing process. Cooperation with this policy is appreciated to facilitate these efforts. Exceptions to this
policy may be made by the Conservation staff if deemed warranted. Please sign and include with your filing. Thank
you.
October 11, 2024

Wetland Summary Letter
100 Beal Street
Hingham, MA 02043

Dear Ms. Botto,
Professional Wetland Scientists (PWS) from Lucas Environmental, LLC (LE) conducted a site investigation
on November 2, 2023 and August 6, 2024 to determine if wetland resources were present at the property
located at 100 Beal Street in Hingham, Massachusetts. Please note that this effort is specific to wetland
resources; it does not evaluate constraints related to local planning or zoning requirements, historical or
cultural significance, nor does it evaluate the potential for soil, air, or water contamination.
The wetland investigation was performed in accordance with the Massachusetts Wetlands Protection Act
(M.G.L. Ch. 131, § 40) and regulations (310 CMR 10.00 et seq.); Section 404 of the Clean Water Act
(33 U.S.C. 1344); Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection (MassDEP) publication
“Massachusetts Handbook for Delineation of Bordering Vegetated Wetlands (2022); and the U.S. Army
Corp of Engineers (USACE) Wetland Delineation Manual (1987); the Northcentral and Northeast Regional
Supplement (2012); and the Town of Hingham Wetlands Protection Bylaw (Article 22) and Wetland
Regulations.
The site investigation was limited to wetland areas within 100 feet and perennial streams within 200 feet of
the site property (the “Study Area”).
The following data sources were examined prior to the site investigation:
•
•
•
•
•
•

Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) Flood Insurance Rate Maps;
United States Geological Survey (USGS) Topographic Quadrangle;
USGS National Map Hydrography Datalayer;
MassGIS MassDEP Wetland and Hydrography Datalayers;
MassGIS Natural Heritage Atlas Datalayers; and
United States Department of Agriculture, Natural Resources Conservation Service (USDA-NRCS)
Soil Survey.

Wetland Summary Letter
1

100 Beal Street
Hingham, Massachusetts

500A Washington Street, Quincy, MA 02169

1.0

EXISTING CONDITIONS

The property, located at 100 Beal Street, includes an apartment building and associated parking area and
driveways located at the northwest end of the property, with the remainder of the approximately 15-acre
parcel consisting of forested uplands and wetlands. The property is bound by Beal Street and residential
development to the north, residential development to the northwest, the Hingham Municipal Lighting Plant
to the east, and undeveloped land of Bare Cove Park to the south and southwest. An unnamed perennial
stream is mapped on the current USGS Topographic Map (Weymouth Quadrangle, 2021) along the
southwest property line and then flows north and west to Beal Cove.
A review of the current MassGIS data layer for the Massachusetts Natural Heritage Atlas (effective
August 1, 2021) under the Natural Heritage and Endangered Species Program (NHESP) indicates that the
Study Area is not located within Priority Habitat of Rare Species or within Estimated Habitat of Rare
Wildlife. A Certified Vernal Pool (CVP #3588) is mapped near the extreme southeast corner of the property.
Portions of the southern and eastern areas of the property are located within the Weymouth Back River
Area of Critical Environmental Concern (ACEC), and the streams and wetlands within and draining to the
ACEC are mapped as Outstanding Resource Waters (ORW). No MassDEP Wellhead Protection Areas or
Watershed Protection Areas are mapped within the Study Area.
According to the July 3, 2024, FEMA Flood Insurance Rate Map (FIRM) for Plymouth County,
Massachusetts, Map Number 25023C0081K, the entire Study Area is located in Zone X, Area of Minimal
Flood Hazard, which is classified as areas outside the 0.2% annual chance floodplain (500-year floodplain).
Therefore, Bordering Land Subject to Flooding (BLSF) is not to be present within the Study Area.

2.0

ENVIRONMENTAL RESOURCE AREAS

Wetland resource areas observed within and near the Study Area include Inland Bank, Bordering Vegetated
Wetlands (BVW), Land Under Water Bodies and Waterways (LUWW), and Riverfront Area (RFA). Three
(3) Isolated Vegetated Wetlands (IVW) are also present within the Study Area. IVWs are not regulated
under the WPA unless the wetland meets the size and volume requirement to be regulated as Isolated Land
Subject to Flooding (ILSF). Although calculations were not performed, it does not appear that the IVW’s
within the Study Area meet the criteria to be regulated as ILSF under the WPA; however, the volume
requirement under the Bylaw (one-sixteenth acre-foot) is less than under the WPA (one-quarter acre-foot).
IVWs are regulated under the Bylaw. Under the Wetlands Protection Act (WPA) and Bylaw, the 100-Foot
Buffer Zone associated with Bank and BVW extends into portions of the Study Area. The 200-Foot
Riverfront Area associated with the unnamed perennial stream also extends into the Study Area.

2.1

Inland Bank – WPA & Bylaw

Section 310 CMR 10.54 of the WPA defines a Bank as the portion of the land surface which normally
abuts and confines a water body. It occurs between a water body and a vegetated bordering wetland and
adjacent flood plain, or, in the absence of these, it occurs between a water body and an upland. The upper
boundary of a Bank is the first observable break in the slope or the mean annual flood level, whichever is
lower. The lower boundary of a Bank is the mean annual low flow level. The delineated Bank of the
perennial stream is described below. The Bylaw does not include any further definition of Bank.

2.2

Bordering Vegetated Wetlands – WPA & Bylaw

Section 310 CMR 10.55 of the WPA defines BVW as “freshwater wetlands which border on creeks, rivers,
streams, ponds and lakes. The types of freshwater wetlands are wet meadows, marshes, swamps and bogs.
Bordering Vegetated Wetlands are areas where the soils are saturated and/or inundated such that they
support a predominance of wetland indicator plants. The boundary of Bordering Vegetated Wetlands is the
line within which 50% or more of the vegetational community consists of wetland indicator plants and
saturated or inundated conditions exist…” The delineated areas of BVW are described below. The Bylaw
definition of Vegetated Wetlands is similar; however, it also includes IVW.

2.3

Land Under Water Bodies and Waterways – WPA & Bylaw

Section 310 CMR 10.56 of the WPA defines LUWW as the land beneath any creek, river, stream, pond or
lake. Said land may be composed of organic muck or peat, fine sediments, rocks or bedrock. The physical
characteristics and location of Land Under Water Bodies and Waterways specified in 310 CMR 10.56(2)(a)
are critical to the protection of the interests specified in 310 CMR 10.56(1). The boundary of Land Under
Water Bodies and Waterways is the mean annual low water level. This resource area is located below the
lower edge of Bank or the Mean Annual High Water (MAHW) line of the perennial stream, therefore it is
not field delineated. The Bylaw does not include any further definition of LUWW relative to rivers or
streams.

2.4

Riverfront Area – WPA & Bylaw

Under Section 310 CMR 10.58 of the WPA, the Riverfront Area is the area of land between a river's mean
annual high-water line measured horizontally (outward from the river and a parallel line located 200 feet
away). The riverfront area may include or overlap other resource areas or their buffer zones. The riverfront
area does not have a buffer zone. Furthermore, the MAHW line is the line that is apparent from visible
markings or changes in the character of soils or vegetation due to the prolonged presence of water and that
distinguishes between predominantly aquatic and predominantly terrestrial land. Field indicators of
bankfull conditions shall be used to determine the mean annual high-water line. Bankfull field indicators
include but are not limited to: changes in slope, changes in vegetation, stain lines, top of pointbars, changes
in bank materials, or bank undercuts. The unnamed stream is depicted as perennial on the most recent
USGS mapping (Weymouth, MA Quadrangle, 2021). Therefore the 200-Foot Riverfront Area extends
landward from the MAHW line, which is coincident with the Inland Bank described below as Stream 1.
The Bylaw definition of Riverfront Area is the same as the WPA.

100 Beal Street
Hingham, Massachusetts

500A Washington Street, Quincy, MA 02169
However, Section 21.1(4) of the Regulations states: “Notwithstanding any provisions of 310 CMR 10.58,
the Commission shall presume that the mean annual high water line of a non-tidal river is coincident with
the outer (landmost) boundary of any Bordering Vegetated Wetland (as defined in these regulations) that
may be adjacent to the river. This presumption may be overcome upon a clear showing that the mean annual
high water line is closer to the river. Such evidence may include hydrological measurements and
calculations prepared by a registered professional engineer and/or hydrologist, and/or stream flow stage
data from U.S. Geological Survey stream gauges and survey. For non-tidal rivers lacking any Bordering
Vegetated Wetland, the inner boundary of the 200-foot Riverfront Area shall be the top of Inland Bank as
determined by the first observable break in slope or the mean annual flood level, whichever is lower.” The
delineated MAHW line has been appropriately identified and delineated within the limits of the BVW.

2.5

Resource Area Descriptions

The following sections describe the delineated resources (BVW, Bank, and Bylaw regulated IVW) that
were identified. BVW Determination Forms were completed and are included with this letter.
Stream 1 – Unnamed Perennial Stream
The unnamed perennial stream flows northwest generally along the western property line, then westerly
away from the Study Area into Beal Cove. The Banks/MAHW line of the northern/eastern streambank was
field delineated with blue survey flagging numbered sequentially from BF1-1 to BF1-36 and BF1-100 to
BF1-123. Vegetation growing along the stream includes red maple (Acer rubrum), sweet pepperbush
(Clethra alnifolia), northern arrowwood (Viburnum recognitum), silky dogwood (Cornus amomum),
northern spicebush (Lindera benzoin), and skunk cabbage (Symplocarpus foetidus).
The MAHW line was delineated based on evidence of bankfull conditions and coincides with Inland Bank.
The Bank along the stream is generally well defined. The stream varies in width from approximately eight
to fifteen feet and observed depths were approximately six to ten inches. The stream bed consists largely
of muck and fine sediments.
Wetland A – BVW
Wetland A is a red maple swamp Palustrine Forested Wetland (PFO) bordering on Stream 1. The wetland
is delineated with pink survey tape numbered sequentially with flag series WFA-1 to WFA-100. Common
vegetation within this wetland includes red maple, northern spicebush, glossy buckthorn (Frangula alnus),
willows (Salix sp.), highbush blueberry (Vaccinium corymbosum), green ash (Fraxinus pennsylvanica),
sweet pepperbush, northern arrowwood, common greenbrier (Smilax rotundifolia), meadowsweet (Spiraea
alba), tussock sedge (Carex stricta), sensitive fern (Onoclea sensibilis), royal fern (Osmunda regalis),
multiflora rose (Rosa multiflora), and skunk cabbage.
The wetland/upland boundary is generally located along a variable topographic break with several areas of
broader transitional zones. Wetland soils consist of deep organic soil (histosol). Indicators of wetland
hydrology include water-stained leaves, shallow soil saturation, free water in the soil test hole, and drainage
patterns.

Wetland Summary Letter
4

100 Beal Street
Hingham, Massachusetts

500A Washington Street, Quincy, MA 02169
Common upland vegetation includes red oak (Quercus rubra), black cherry (Prunus serotina), white pine
(Pinus strobus), Norway maple (Acer platanoides), white oak (Quercus alba), gray birch (Betula
alleghaniensis), American hop-hornbeam (Ostrya virginiana), American beech (Fagus grandifolia),
staghorn sumac (Rhus typhina), Oriental bittersweet (Celastrus orbiculatus), Tatarian honeysuckle
(Lonicera tatarica), multiflora rose, American pokeweed (Phytolacca americana), garlic mustard (Alliaria
petiolata), and tall goldenrod (Solidago altissima).
Wetland B – BVW
Wetland B is a PFO located in the west-central portion of the Study Area between Beal Street and
Wetland A. The wetland is delineated with pink survey tape numbered sequentially with flag series WFB-1
to WFB-23. Common vegetation consists primarily of American elm (Ulmus americana), common
buckthorn (Rhamnus cathartica), northern arrowwood, common greenbrier, and Tatarian honeysuckle.
Soils generally consist of a depleted matrix and redoximorphic features under a dark A horizon. Indicators
of wetland hydrology include shallow soil saturation, inundation, and drainage patterns. Water flows
through this wetland via culverts located at the north and south ends of the wetland and drains to Wetland A.
Wetland C – IVW
Wetland C is a small Palustrine Scrub-Shrub (PSS) wetland located just off-site along the northeast corner
of the property. The wetland boundary was delineated with pink survey tape numbered sequentially with
flag series WFC-1 to WFC-6. Plant species observed include primarily willow and glossy buckthorn. Soils
have been excavated and are shallow with depletions.
Wetland D – IVW
Wetland D is a small PFO wetland located along the property line and Beal Street. The wetland boundary
was delineated with pink survey tape numbered sequentially with flag series WFD-1 to WFD-6. Vegetation
observed includes red maple, glossy buckthorn, northern arrowwood, common greenbrier, and poison ivy.
Observed soil consists of a deep, dark A-horizon over a B-horizon with a depleted matrix. Hydrological
indicators include water-stained leaves.
Wetland E – BVW
Wetland E is located off-site on the north side of Beal Street and consists of a drainage swale that drains to
a culvert under Beal Street. The southern end of the wetland swale was delineated with pink survey tape
numbered sequentially with flag series WFE-1 to WFE-4.

2.6

Hingham Wetlands Protection Bylaw

Under the Hingham Wetlands Protection Bylaw: “The intent of the Conservation Commission is to move
all structures and activities as far away as possible from any Resource Area, in order to protect the wetland
values of Resource Areas. Except as otherwise specified, Resource Area buffers shall be retained and
maintained in a naturally vegetated condition. Where buffer disturbance has occurred during construction,
revegetation with native vegetation may be required. The Commission may require that already-altered
buffer zone be restored in order to protect or improve Resource Area values. Restoration means planting

native vegetation, grading, correcting site drainage, removing debris, or other measures which will
improve, restore and protect the wetland values of the Resource Area.”
The Bylaw Regulations define project-specific performance standards and setbacks for septic systems,
pools and tennis courts, landscaping, docks and piers, underground storage tanks, filling, and structures.

# Architectural Plans, Civil Engineering Drawings, Site Plans, and ANRAD Filings Overview

**Location:** 100 Beal Street, Hingham, MA 02043 (Plymouth County; Assessor Map 58, Lot 23)  
**Applicant / Proponent:** Hingham Housing Authority (in partnership with Peabody Properties / Affordable Housing Services Collaborative, Inc. - AHSC)  
**Primary Engineering & Environmental Firms:**
- **Weston & Sampson:** Site planning, civil engineering, landscape architecture, sustainable stormwater infrastructure, pollinator habitat design
- **Lucas Environmental, LLC (LE):** Professional wetland scientists, ANRAD narrative & wetland boundary delineation
- **Control Point Associates, Inc. (CPA):** ALTA/NSPS land title survey, topographic mapping, wetland flag boundary instrument survey
- **Bohler Engineering, Inc.:** Associated engineering consultation
- **GM2 Associates, Inc.:** Earlier due diligence, conceptual layout (50 units), initial site evaluation, ANR subdivision planning

Based on the ultra-high-resolution March 3, 2026 site plan update (`20260303-Beal-Street-Housing-Rendered-Plan-Update.jpg`) and architectural renderings:

- **Building Massing & Typology:**
  - 3-story modern residential building footprint specifically designed to step into the natural woodland topography.
  - Total unit capacity: 68 senior affordable rental apartments (advancing from earlier 50-unit and 60-unit conceptual iterations).
  - Dedicated common amenity spaces: central multi-purpose community hall, wellness suite, quiet reading rooms, administrative management office, and package reception.
- **Site Access & Circulation:**
  - Main vehicular ingress/egress from Beal Street through an improved, traffic-calmed curb cut.
  - Surface parking carefully arranged along the northern and interior facade, avoiding intrusion into the 50-foot wetland setback.
  - Full perimeter ADA-compliant paved multi-use walking loop connecting to outdoor recreation zones and Bare Cove Park paths.
- **Landscape Architecture & Stormwater:**
  - Low Impact Development (LID) bio-retention swales, rain gardens, and subterranean infiltration chambers engineered to protect the Weymouth Back River watershed.
  - Native pollinator gardens, sensory planting zones, shade trees to mitigate urban heat island effects, and a resident raised-bed garden patio.
  - Outdoor gathering terraces featuring shade pergolas and bench positioning.

## Article: 2025-04-18_opinion_how_will_we_honor_environmental_legacy_v1.md

# OPINION: How will we honor the environmental legacy of our forebears?

- **Publication:** The Hingham Anchor
- **Date:** 2025-04-18T09:57:59
- **Original URL:** https://www.hinghamanchor.com/opinion-how-will-we-honor-the-environmental-legacy-of-our-forebears/

---

![](https://www.hinghamanchor.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Screen-Shot-2025-04-18-at-9.49.00-AM-1024x1014.png)

**April 18, 2025 By Anita Bapooji Ryan**

Hingham is rich in history! As we approach Town Meeting and a vote on the location of the new $35 million dollar senior center, I wanted to re-visit some of Hingham’s environmental history to protect Bare Cove Park. As many of you know, the US government conveyed a parcel of land along the Back River to Hingham in 1972 as part of its Land to Parks program. Recognizing the environmental significance of this land, [Hingham and Weymouth residents formed the Back River Committee](https://backriverwatershed.org/a-tale-of-two-marys) in 1978 to further understand and protect this watershed and its surrounding ecosystem. That work led to a nomination in 1982 to the Massachusetts Executive Office of Environmental Affairs for designation of the Back River and its surrounding land as an Area of Critical Environmental Concern (“ACEC”). The ACEC designation is for locations in Massachusetts that receive special recognition because of the quality, uniqueness and significance of their natural resources. There are only 30 ACECs in the state and Hingham is blessed to have two of them – [Back River ACEC](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/weymouth-back-river-acec) and [Weir River ACEC](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/weir-river-acec).

In doing its work over a 4-year period, the Back River Committee engaged in considerable study and discussion before selecting the area to nominate as an ACEC. The parcel selected was the **“most critical or sensitive to development pressures.**” The ACEC nomination was championed by the Town of Hingham’s Select Board [(chair Eugene Bickford](https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/bostonglobe/name/eugene-bickford-obituary?id=27977213)), Conservation Commission (chair Robert Beal Jr.), Planning Board ([chair Richard S. Cook](https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/wickedlocal-hingham/name/richard-cook-obituary?id=7065581)), and Bare Cove Committee ([chair John P. Richardson](https://www.downingchapel.com/obituary/JohnPeabody-Richardson)). In the official [designation of the Back River ACEC](https://www.mass.gov/doc/designation-weymouth-back-river-estuary-acec/download) signed by the then Secretary of Environmental Affairs, [John Bewick](https://www.bostonglobe.com/metro/obituaries/2015/01/05/john-bewick-served-massachusetts-secretary-environmental-affairs/EEOPVH3vd7W0DHyJFivNHO/story.html) (husband of Martha Reardon Bewick), himself a Hingham resident, he pointed out that “the resources of the Back River, its surrounding lands and portions of its water shed have remained largely unaltered despite the generally urban setting” and that it **“remains a natural area in the midst of expanding urban/suburban development.”**

Opening page of the Back River ACEC Nomination

![](https://www.hinghamanchor.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Screen-Shot-2025-04-18-at-9.54.18-AM-829x1024.png)

The Back River Committee’s concerns in 1982 about development pressures were certainly clairvoyant.

Since the Back River achieved ACEC status, the surrounding land has steadily been developed:
Hingham Woods – 1985 (277 units)
Conservatory Park – 1990s (over 85 homes)
Adams Court – 2003 (14 homes)
Baker Hill/Hill Top – 2005 (45 homes)
Carlson Fields – 2007
Hingham DPW – 2009
Back River Condos – 2013 (27 homes)
Taylor Lane – 2013 (8 homes)
Hingham Light Plant – 2015
Weathervane Court (23 homes) – 2015
The Cove – 2020 (220 units)

All of these developments demonstrate a key fact – the Hingham residents who worked on the ACEC nomination were balanced in their approach and were not environmentally-greedy. They could have tried to get more undeveloped land in the surrounding area in Hingham to be part of the ACEC but they didn’t. Instead they were true to the mandate – protect the “areas of critical environmental concern.” Now the Town of Hingham wants to build inside of that ACEC as quickly as possible. Hingham’s proposed new senior center, covering a total of 128,000 square feet (28,000 sq feet building plus 200- space asphalt parking lot) will require the removal and disturbance of forest and conservation land within the Back River ACEC and within Bare Cove Park.

I am not providing this information because I am against the Town having a new senior center. I am concerned that we ended up proposing to destroy part of a densely forested and critical environmental area, when the Town previously worked so hard to advocate for its protection. There are alternative and more central locations for our senior center that don’t result in deforestation. I also don’t understand why we think it’s ok to construct in this sensitive area when the biggest threat to wildlife is habitat loss.

Tucker’s swamp used to be filled with Blue Heron and it isn’t anymore. I also find this habitat loss troubling considering there’s no synergies with the proposed senior center; it currently is for the exclusive use of those 60+ on Monday through Thursday. The remaining 40% of the week the senior center is closed, and if built, its 200-space asphalt parking lot would sit empty.

Supporting letters for ACEC nomination from Hingham Land Conservation Trust and Select Board:

![](https://www.hinghamanchor.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Screen-Shot-2025-04-18-at-9.55.37-AM-1024x459.png)

I am also finding it hard to reconcile our Tree City USA recognition, with the deforestation that construction of this senior center would cause. This is the same Town that passed a passed plastic bottle ban, a plastic bag ban, developed a 2023 Climate Action Plan a core component of which is the preservation of natural resources, and at our upcoming Town Meeting, seeks to implement a specialized building code to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Simply put, are we fair-weather environmentalists?

The Town of Hingham’s 2023 Climate Action Plan is an important roadmap in our continuous stance against climate change. It warns us that buildings make up 68% of Hingham’s total carbon emissions. It warns us that transportation generates the second largest source of emissions. Yet we’re now proposing a senior center in the far north corner of Hingham (almost in Weymouth) necessitating most seniors to drive through or across town, which contributes to more carbon emissions. Accommodating 200 parking spots encourages single-driver car trips (while our 2023 Climate Action Plan presses us to “encourage carpooling/ride sharing because this is a long-standing means of removing vehicles from the roads.”). A more centralized location for the senior center would serve easier access (walking or biking) and less cross-town driving for our seniors, and our environment would benefit.

How do we get people to cherish what they take for granted? Environmentalists show people what they are losing and hope they’ll realize it before it’s too late. Time and time again, short term wants lose against long term needs. Our forebears in Hingham worked hard to show us the way and their hard work has protected the Back River ACEC — up until today. Let’s honor their legacy by not allowing it to be dismantled.

VOTE NO TO ARTICLE 15 AND SAVE BARE COVE PARK FROM DEVELOPMENT!

![](https://www.hinghamanchor.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Screen-Shot-2025-04-18-at-9.56.26-AM-1024x528.png)John Bewick (MA Office of Environmental Affairs), Majorie O’Malley (Coastal Zone Management) and Mary Toomey at the Back River ACEC designation on September 10, 1982
